name: Skill Diagnostic
source: Original difficulty-ladder questions written for LSAT Trainer. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: At the Larkhill Community Woodshop, any piece of furniture that is to be varnished in the finishing room must first be sanded by a staff member. No staff member sands a piece until it has been left in the drying room for at least a week after gluing. Tomas's bookcase was varnished in the finishing room this morning.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Tomas's bookcase was sanded by a staff member at some point within the past week.
Tomas's bookcase was left in the drying room for at least a week after it was glued.
Every piece left in the drying room for at least a week after gluing will be sanded by a staff member.
Any piece that a staff member at the woodshop has sanded will eventually be varnished in the finishing room.
Tomas's bookcase was not varnished on the same day that a staff member sanded it.
questions.explanation: Core move: follow a two-link chain forward from a known fact. Varnishing requires sanding, and sanding requires a week in the drying room, so Tomas's varnished bookcase must have spent at least a week drying, which is (B). The most tempting traps are (C) and (D), which run the rules backward: a week of drying is required for sanding, not a guarantee of it, and sanding is required for varnishing, not a promise of it. (A) and (E) make claims about timing that the rules never fix.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Varnished → sanded by staff first; 2. Sanded → left in the drying room at least a week after gluing; 3. Tomas's bookcase was varnished this morning.

breakdown.analysis: Two rules, one fact. Chain them: varnished → sanded → a week in the drying room. Tomas's bookcase was varnished, so it rides the whole chain to the end. Prephrase: the bookcase was sanded, and it sat in the drying room for at least a week. The traps will flip an arrow. 'Must first be' and 'no ... until' both introduce necessary conditions, not guarantees. It's like 'you can't board without a ticket': having a ticket doesn't mean you boarded.

choices.note: We don't know this. The rules say the bookcase was sanded before it was varnished, but not when. It could have been sanded a month ago.
CORRECT. Varnished → sanded → a week in the drying room. The bookcase was varnished, so it dried for at least a week.

Tempting, because it uses the exact words of rule 2. But it reverses it. A week of drying is needed before sanding; it doesn't guarantee that a piece gets sanded. Some pieces may sit in the drying room forever.
This reverses rule 1. Sanding is required before varnishing, but nothing says every sanded piece gets varnished. Plenty of furniture is left unvarnished, or painted instead.
We don't know this. 'Must first be sanded' fixes the order, not the gap between the steps. Same-day sanding and varnishing is never ruled out.

questions.stimulus: No member of the Ostrander Rowing Club steers a racing crew unless he or she has completed the club's coxswain course, and everyone who has completed that course has served at least one shift on the club's safety launch. Any member who has steered a racing crew is entitled to vote on the club's regatta schedule. Corinne, a member, has never served a shift on the safety launch.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Corinne is not entitled to vote on the regatta schedule that the club's members adopt.
Every member who has served a shift on the safety launch has completed the club's coxswain course.
Any member who is entitled to vote on the club's regatta schedule has steered a racing crew.
Corinne has not steered a racing crew for the club at any time since she became a member.
Most members who have completed the club's coxswain course have at some point steered a racing crew.
questions.explanation: Core move: the contrapositive of a chain. Steering a crew requires the coxswain course, and the course requires a shift on the safety launch, so a member with no launch shift has not completed the course and cannot have steered a crew, which is (D). The tempting trap is (A): it treats steering a crew as the only route to a vote, but the rule only says steering is enough for a vote, so Corinne might qualify some other way. (B) and (C) each reverse one of the rules.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Steer a racing crew → completed the coxswain course; 2. Completed the course → served a shift on the safety launch; 3. Steered a crew → may vote on the regatta schedule; 4. Corinne has never served a launch shift.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: steer a crew → coxswain course → launch shift. Contrapositive: no launch shift → no course → never steered a crew. Corinne has no launch shift, so she never completed the course and never steered a crew. Prephrase: Corinne hasn't steered a crew (or hasn't completed the course). The trap is rule 3. Steering a crew gets you a vote, but it's not the only way to get one. Knowing Corinne didn't steer tells you nothing about her vote.

choices.note: Tempting. This is the next step most people take, and it's wrong. 'Steered → can vote' gives a sufficient condition. Failing it doesn't block the vote; maybe officers or long-time members can vote too. That's a classic negation error.
This reverses rule 2. Completing the course requires a launch shift; it doesn't follow that everyone who served a shift took the course.
This reverses rule 3. Steering a crew is enough for a vote, not required for one.
CORRECT. No launch shift → no course → never steered a crew. Corinne can't have steered one.
We don't know this. The rules say nothing about how many course graduates actually steer crews. It could be none.

questions.stimulus: Library administrator: The board of the Brenton Public Library votes on every program for which the library pays an outside presenter; programs run by staff or volunteers go ahead without a vote. The board never voted on this summer's astronomy series. So the astronomy series cannot have been eligible for the county's arts-partnership grants.
questions.stem: The administrator's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every program for which the library itself pays an outside presenter is eligible for the county's arts-partnership grants.
Most programs that are eligible for the county's arts-partnership grants are programs that the library's board has voted on.
The board votes only on those programs on which the library's own rules require the board to hold a vote.
No program that the board has voted on has ever received any one of the county's arts-partnership grants.
Only programs for which the library pays an outside presenter are eligible for the county's arts-partnership grants.
questions.explanation: Core move: build the missing link of a chain in the right direction. The premises give 'no board vote → no paid outside presenter' (contrapositive of the first rule), and the conclusion needs 'no paid outside presenter → not eligible', which is what (E) says: only programs with a paid outside presenter are eligible. The most tempting trap is (A), which joins the same two ideas but backward; knowing that paid-presenter programs are eligible says nothing about a program without one. (B) is too weak, since 'most' leaves room for the astronomy series to be an eligible program the board never voted on.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The astronomy series was not eligible for the county's arts-partnership grants.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The board votes on every program with a paid outside presenter; staff- and volunteer-run programs get no vote; the board never voted on the astronomy series.

breakdown.analysis: So the series had no paid outside presenter. Why does that make it ineligible? The argument never says. Chain: paid presenter → board vote. Contrapositive: no board vote → no paid presenter. Conclusion: not eligible. Missing link: no paid presenter → not eligible, which is the same as eligible → paid presenter. Full chain for the series: no vote → no paid presenter → not eligible. Prephrase: 'Only programs with a paid outside presenter are eligible.'

choices.note: Tempting, because it links the right two ideas. But it points the wrong way: paid presenter → eligible. The series had no paid presenter, so this rule never applies to it.
Too weak. If only most eligible programs get a vote, the series could be one of the eligible programs the board skipped.
Irrelevant. This tells us why the board might skip a program, but nothing about grant eligibility.
Wrong direction. It's about programs the board did vote on. The series wasn't voted on, so this says nothing about it.
CORRECT. Eligible → paid presenter, so no paid presenter → not eligible. The series had no vote, so no paid presenter, so it wasn't eligible.

questions.stimulus: At Bellbrook Hospital, every nurse assigned to the cardiac unit is certified in advanced life support. A nurse who works only night shifts may be assigned to the cardiac unit only if he or she has at least five years of nursing experience. All of the hospital's nurses with five or more years of experience serve on its training rotation, and no one on the training rotation works only night shifts.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: At least one of the nurses assigned to Bellbrook's cardiac unit is certified in advanced life support and works only night shifts.
Some Bellbrook nurse who works only night shifts is certified in advanced life support despite having fewer than five years of experience.
Some nurse assigned to Bellbrook's cardiac unit has fewer than five years of nursing experience and does not serve on the training rotation.
Some nurse who serves on the training rotation is neither certified in advanced life support nor assigned to the cardiac unit.
Every nurse at Bellbrook who works only night shifts has fewer than five years of nursing experience.
questions.explanation: Core move: chain the rules until one combination loops back on itself. A night-only nurse in the cardiac unit needs five years' experience, five years puts a nurse on the training rotation, and no one on the rotation works only nights, so the nurse in (A) cannot exist; the certification detail is camouflage, since every cardiac nurse is certified anyway. Most students pick (C) because the five-year rule feels like a rule for the whole cardiac unit, but it is triggered only by working only night shifts, so a day-shift cardiac nurse with two years' experience who is off the rotation breaks nothing. (E) sounds restrictive, but it must be true (five years → rotation → not night-only), and whatever must be true can be true.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Cardiac unit → ALS certified; 2. Night-only AND cardiac unit → 5+ years; 3. 5+ years → training rotation; 4. Training rotation → not night-only.

breakdown.analysis: Four rules and a CANNOT stem: so what kind of nurse can't exist? Look for a chain that runs into a wall. Start with a night-only nurse in the cardiac unit: night-only + cardiac → 5+ years → rotation → NOT night-only. That nurse would have to be night-only and not night-only at once, so no cardiac nurse works only nights. Rules 3 and 4 also give a free inference: night-only → under 5 years. We need the answer that describes the impossible nurse, possibly dressed up with extra details. Most students pick (C), because the five-year rule feels like it governs the whole cardiac unit; it fails because rule 2 is triggered only by night-only nurses. Read the trigger, not the topic.

choices.note: CORRECT. Strip out the certification detail (every cardiac nurse is certified anyway) and you have a night-only cardiac nurse. Night-only + cardiac → 5+ years → rotation → not night-only. Contradiction, so this nurse can't exist.

Can be true. Rules 3 and 4 actually force every night-only nurse to have under five years, so this is a perfectly legal nurse as long as she works outside the cardiac unit. Nothing ties certification to shifts.

Tempting, and the trap most people fall into. The five-year rule sounds like a cardiac-unit rule, but its trigger is 'works only night shifts.' A day-shift cardiac nurse with two years' experience violates nothing, and the rotation is required only of nurses with 5+ years, so being off it is fine too.
Can be true. Certification is required only for the cardiac unit, and the rotation rules say nothing about it. A rotation nurse who works elsewhere needn't be certified.
Must be true (5+ years → rotation → not night-only, so night-only → under 5 years), and anything that must be true can be true. It sounds restrictive, which is why it draws people on a CANNOT stem.

questions.stimulus: Budget director: Under Rellford's budget policy, any city department that finishes the fiscal year under budget receives a bonus allocation the following year. Critics charge that the parks department's bonus allocation is undeserved, since a department can easily come in under budget by deferring required maintenance. But the city auditor flags every department that defers required maintenance, and the auditor did not flag the parks department. So the parks department's bonus allocation is deserved.
questions.stem: The budget director's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: If a city department finishes the fiscal year under budget by deferring its required maintenance, then its bonus allocation is undeserved.
Most departments that are not flagged by the city auditor deserve the bonus allocations that they receive under the policy.
A city department's bonus allocation is deserved unless that department came in under budget by deferring its required maintenance.
No department can finish the fiscal year under budget merely by deferring all of the maintenance it is required to perform.
Departments that the city auditor does not flag are more likely than flagged departments to have earned their bonus allocations legitimately.
questions.explanation: Core move: proving a positive ('deserved') takes a rule that makes deferring maintenance the only thing that could spoil a bonus. The premises show parks did not defer required maintenance (deferring → flagged; parks wasn't flagged), and (C), read as 'no deferral → deserved,' turns that fact straight into the conclusion. Most students pick (A) because it restates the critics' standard in nearly the same words, but (A) only says when a bonus is undeserved; since parks didn't defer, (A) is never triggered and can't show the bonus is deserved. (B) and (E) fail on strength, since parks could be one of the unflagged departments whose bonus is still undeserved.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The parks department's bonus allocation is deserved.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Defers required maintenance → flagged by the auditor; parks was not flagged; so parks did not defer required maintenance. (Critics: deferring maintenance can make a bonus undeserved.)

breakdown.analysis: So parks didn't defer maintenance. Why does that make its bonus deserved? Maybe a bonus can be undeserved for some other reason, like creative accounting. The premises rule out only one way a bonus could go bad. The bridge we need: no deferral → deserved (contrapositive: undeserved → deferral). 'X unless Y' means 'if not Y, then X,' so 'deserved unless it deferred maintenance' is exactly that bridge. Chain: not flagged → didn't defer → (bridge) → deserved. Most students pick (A) because it repeats the critics' rule; but it runs the wrong way. Deferral → undeserved can show that a bonus is undeserved, never that one is deserved. Worth knowing: 'if' and 'unless' can sit in nearly identical sentences and say opposite things.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It runs deferral → undeserved. Parks didn't defer, so this rule is never triggered and says nothing about parks. Concluding 'deserved' from it would be negating the sufficient condition. It feels on point because it's the critics' own standard.
Too weak. 'Most' unflagged departments deserve their bonuses, but parks might be in the minority that doesn't. A sufficient assumption has to guarantee the conclusion.
CORRECT. 'Deserved unless deferral' = no deferral → deserved. Parks wasn't flagged → didn't defer → bonus deserved. The conclusion now follows. The unless-form is the disguise.
This attacks the critics' premise, but undercutting the critics doesn't prove the bonus is deserved. The bonus could be undeserved for some other reason.
Too weak. 'More likely' is a probability across departments. It can't make the conclusion follow for parks in particular.

questions.stimulus:
Ines: The Pembrook ferry service should replace its diesel boats with electric ones right away. Electric boats are cleaner, quieter, and cheaper to run.

Garrett: Electric boats are certainly cleaner and quieter. But no electric boat now available can make the crossing in a winter storm, so switching now would leave the island cut off for days at a time. The ferry service should wait.
questions.stem: Ines and Garrett disagree over whether
choices: the Pembrook ferry service should replace its diesel boats with electric ones now
electric boats are cleaner and quieter than the ferry service’s diesel boats
electric boats are cheaper to run than the ferry service’s diesel boats
winter storms on the Pembrook crossing are becoming more frequent
island residents would accept being cut off for a few days in exchange for a cleaner ferry
questions.explanation: Core move: find the claim one speaker affirms and the other denies. Ines says the service should switch right away; Garrett says it should wait, so they disagree over A. The most tempting trap is C, because cost is one of Ines's reasons; but Garrett never addresses cost, and to disagree, both speakers must take a side. Garrett explicitly agrees with B, and neither speaker addresses D or E.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ines: Switch to electric boats right away; they're cleaner, quieter, and cheaper to run; Garrett: Granted, cleaner and quieter, but none can cross in a winter storm, so switching now would strand the island; wait.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Ines: switch now. Garrett: wait. That's a clean yes/no. Notice what Garrett grants ('certainly cleaner and quieter') and what he skips (cost). Things he grants are agreements; things he skips can't be disagreements.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ines says replace them right away; Garrett says wait. Yes versus no.
They agree. Garrett says electric boats are 'certainly cleaner and quieter.'
Tempting, since cost is one of Ines's reasons. But Garrett never mentions cost. Silence isn't disagreement. You can't disagree about something you never addressed.
Neither speaker says storms are getting more frequent. Garrett only says current electric boats can't handle them.
Neither speaker discusses what residents would accept. Ines doesn't even admit the island would be cut off.

questions.stimulus:
Hanne: Attendance at our community theater has fallen by a fifth this year. We should lower our ticket prices.

Petr: The drop has nothing to do with our prices. The Dorn Playhouse charges even more than we do, and its attendance rose this year.
questions.stem: Petr’s response to Hanne is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that lowering ticket prices would increase the theater's total revenue for the season
draws a conclusion about all theatergoers from a sample of patrons who are unlikely to be representative
attacks Hanne's motives for proposing lower prices rather than addressing the reasoning behind her proposal
overlooks the possibility that the two theaters differ in ways other than price that affect attendance
takes for granted that the theater's attendance will continue to fall unless something about the theater is changed
questions.explanation: Core move: spot an uneven comparison used to rule out a cause. Petr concludes that price can't explain his theater's decline because a pricier theater did well, but the Dorn Playhouse may have better shows, a better location, or other advantages that outweigh its prices (D). The most tempting trap is A, which describes a weakness in the conversation, but it's Hanne's proposal that relies on lower prices helping, and the question asks about Petr's response. E also describes an assumption Hanne might make, not Petr.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Petr) The attendance drop has nothing to do with prices.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Petr) The Dorn Playhouse charges more, and its attendance rose.

breakdown.analysis: So the Dorn charges more and is doing fine. Does that prove price doesn't matter here? Only if the two theaters are alike in every other way. Maybe the Dorn has bigger stars, a downtown location, or a hit show. Then price could still be hurting Hanne's theater; the Dorn just has something that outweighs it. It's like saying 'that restaurant is pricier than ours and packed, so our prices can't be why we're empty,' when that restaurant has a famous chef. We need an answer that says Petr ignores other differences between the theaters.

choices.note: Tempting, because something like this is a fair question to ask in this conversation. But it's about Hanne's proposal. Petr never says anything about revenue. Read the stem: it asks about Petr's response.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We should cut our prices in half; that will obviously bring in more money.

choices.note: No sample of theatergoers is involved. Petr compares two theaters.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The five patrons I asked at opening night said prices are fine, so no one in town thinks our prices are too high.

choices.note: Petr never mentions Hanne's motives. He addresses her claim directly.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Hanne only wants lower prices because her friends would get in cheaper, so we can ignore her.

choices.note: CORRECT. Petr uses one pricier theater's success to rule out price as a cause, without considering that the Dorn may have other advantages, like better shows or a better location, that more than offset its prices.
Petr doesn't predict anything about future attendance. If anyone assumes the drop will continue, it's Hanne.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Attendance fell this year, so it will keep falling every year unless we act.

questions.stimulus:
Lucia: The Hollin Seed Bank should let home gardeners borrow seed of its rare varieties. If gardeners keep those varieties growing, the varieties will survive even if the bank’s freezers someday fail.

Arno: Having rare varieties grown outside the vault is certainly worthwhile. But gardeners’ plants will cross-pollinate with nearby plants, so any seed they return would no longer be true to type. The bank should instead pay a few trained growers to raise rare varieties in isolated plots.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Lucia and Arno agree that
choices: seed returned to the seed bank by home gardeners would not be true to type
the seed bank's freezers are likely to fail at some point in the coming years
at least some rare varieties should be grown outside the seed bank's vault
trained growers would keep rare varieties true to type more reliably than home gardeners would
preserving rare varieties is the most important of the seed bank's many functions
questions.explanation: Core move: for agreement, each speaker must be committed to the claim, not merely not deny it. Lucia's plan has gardeners growing rare varieties and Arno's has trained growers doing so, and Arno calls outside growing 'worthwhile,' so both are committed to C. The most tempting trap is D, which Arno clearly believes, but Lucia says nothing about trained growers or seed purity. B overreads Lucia's 'even if … someday,' which is a hedge, not a prediction, and A is Arno's objection, which Lucia never accepts.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Lucia: Lend rare-variety seed to home gardeners so the varieties survive even if the freezers fail; Arno: Outside growing is worthwhile, but gardeners' plants will cross-pollinate; pay trained growers to raise them in isolated plots instead.

breakdown.analysis: They disagree on WHO should grow the rare varieties. But both plans have the varieties grown outside the vault, and Arno says outright that's worthwhile. Agreement questions punish answers only one speaker holds. Test each choice: would Lucia sign it? Would Arno? Both must say yes.

choices.note: Only Arno. This is his objection to Lucia's plan, and she never accepts it.
Neither commits to this. Lucia says 'even if the freezers someday fail,' which is a precaution, not a prediction.
CORRECT. Lucia's plan has gardeners grow them; Arno's has trained growers grow them. Different methods, same goal: rare varieties grown outside the vault.
Tempting. Arno clearly believes this; it's his whole reason for preferring trained growers. But Lucia never mentions trained growers or seed purity. One speaker's view isn't agreement.
Too strong. Neither speaker ranks the seed bank's functions.

questions.stimulus:
Odile: The Marsh Lane mill's new dye cannot be what has been turning the Fennick River cloudy. The mill uses that dye only on days when it runs a second shift, and the river has turned cloudy on several days with no second shift.

Bastien: You assume the dye could affect the river only on days it is used. But the mill collects its rinse water in holding ponds and releases it into the river once a week, regardless of which shifts have run.
questions.stem: Bastien's argument proceeds by
choices: asserting that the mill's new dye is in fact what has been turning the Fennick River cloudy
showing that the evidence Odile cites is compatible with the very possibility she takes it to rule out
disputing Odile's claim that the mill uses the new dye only on days when it runs a second shift
charging that Odile treats a condition that is necessary for the river's cloudiness as though it were sufficient for it
suggesting that the river's cloudiness on certain days was caused by something other than the mill's operations
questions.explanation: Core move: describe a reply that removes an argument's support without asserting the opposite conclusion. Odile clears the dye because the river clouded on days it wasn't used; Bastien shows how the dye could still reach the river on those days, through the weekly pond release, so her evidence fits perfectly well with the dye being the cause, which (B) says abstractly. Most students pick (A) because Bastien plainly suspects the dye; but he never claims it is the culprit, only that Odile's evidence doesn't clear it, and undercutting an argument isn't proving its opposite. (D) sounds sophisticated, but Bastien's point is about delayed timing, not a confusion of necessary and sufficient conditions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Odile) The new dye can't be what is clouding the river.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Odile) The dye is used only on second-shift days; the river clouded on days with no second shift. (Bastien) You assume the dye acts only on days it's used; rinse water is held in ponds and released weekly no matter which shifts ran.

breakdown.analysis: Odile's logic: if the dye caused it, the river would cloud only on dye days. It clouded on non-dye days, so not the dye. Bastien attacks the 'only on dye days' assumption: the dye sits in ponds and gets released later. So cloudiness on a non-dye day is no evidence against the dye. Does he say the dye IS the cause? No. He just takes away Odile's reason for clearing it. It's like saying 'the cake can't have made me sick, because I got sick on a day I didn't eat any,' and a friend pointing out that you ate the leftovers. The right answer may describe this abstractly. Most students pick (A), mistaking 'your evidence doesn't clear it' for 'it's guilty.'

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Bastien sounds like he suspects the dye, and he might. But he never claims it IS the cause; he only shows Odile's evidence doesn't clear it. Undercutting an argument isn't proving its opposite.
choices.example: Example of method: Water samples taken on every cloudy day contained the new dye, so the dye is what's clouding the river.

choices.note: CORRECT. Odile's evidence (cloudy on non-dye days) is supposed to rule out the dye. Bastien shows that evidence is consistent with the dye being the cause, via the weekly pond release. Abstract wording, exact description.
No. Bastien accepts that the dye is used only on second-shift days. His point is about when it reaches the river.
choices.example: Example of method: Actually, the mill uses that dye on most weekdays, whether or not a second shift runs.

choices.note: Sounds like something a sharp critic would say. But Bastien's point is about timing, a delayed release. He doesn't accuse Odile of confusing necessary and sufficient conditions.
choices.example: Example of method: You show the dye must be present for the river to cloud, but that doesn't mean the dye alone is enough to cloud it.

choices.note: Opposite direction. Bastien's point keeps the mill in the picture; he doesn't offer a non-mill cause.
choices.example: Example of method: The cloudiness on those days came from runoff after heavy rain upstream, not from anything the mill did.

questions.stimulus:
Hollis: The Tarrow library's junior chess program has clearly raised its participants' math grades. Children who joined last fall improved their math grades this year more than classmates who did not join.

Priya: Joining may well improve children's math grades, but your evidence doesn't show it. Parents who enroll children in after-school chess are also the parents most likely to push them in math. So that gap could exist even if the program did nothing.
questions.stem: Hollis and Priya disagree over whether
choices: the junior chess program raised the math grades of the children who joined it
children who joined the program improved their math grades more than their classmates who did not
parents who enroll their children in after-school chess programs tend to push them in math
after-school chess programs generally improve the school performance of the children who take part
the participants' greater math improvement, compared with that of their classmates, establishes that the program raised their grades
questions.explanation: Core move: separate disagreement about a conclusion from disagreement about whether the evidence proves it. Hollis says the improvement gap shows the program raised grades; Priya says the gap doesn't show that, since it could exist even if the program did nothing, so they disagree over (E). Most students pick (A), which differs from (E) only in dropping 'establishes'; Priya explicitly allows that joining 'may well' improve grades, so she never denies that the program did. (B) is a fact Priya accepts, and (C) is asserted only by Priya.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Hollis: participants improved more than classmates, so the program clearly raised their grades; Priya: maybe it did, but the gap doesn't show it, since pushy parents could produce the same gap.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Does Priya say the program didn't raise grades? No: 'Joining may well improve children's math grades.' She attacks the evidence, not the conclusion. Hollis says the gap clearly shows the effect; Priya says it doesn't show it. So the point at issue is whether the evidence proves the claim. Most students pick (A), the claim itself; but Priya stays neutral on it, so she can't be on the 'no' side.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap: it's Hollis's conclusion, and Priya clearly pushes back. But she pushes back on the proof, not the claim; she says joining 'may well' improve grades. She takes no 'no' position here.
Both accept it. Priya grants the gap and explains it differently.
Only Priya says this. Hollis never addresses parents.
Neither speaker talks about chess programs in general or about school performance beyond math.
CORRECT. Hollis: the gap shows the program raised grades ('clearly'). Priya: 'your evidence doesn't show it.' Yes vs. no on exactly this.

questions.stimulus: Councillor Brandt: The engineering consultant who recommends that Port Sallow build a seawall along its harbor stands to gain from that recommendation, since her firm would be hired to design the wall if it were built. We should therefore reject her conclusion that a seawall is the best way to protect the harbor from storm surges.
questions.stem: The reasoning in Councillor Brandt's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that a seawall would cost the town more than other forms of storm protection
overlooks the possibility that the consultant's firm could also profit from designing some other kind of storm-protection project
takes for granted that storm surges pose a serious threat to Port Sallow's harbor and its shipping
infers that the consultant's conclusion should be rejected merely because she would gain if it were accepted
relies on the opinion of an expert whose expertise lies outside the field that is under discussion
questions.explanation: Core move: spot an attack on the source in its quietest form, a possible motive. Brandt never touches the consultant's reasons; he infers that her conclusion should be rejected only from the fact that her firm would profit, which is what (D) says. A person with a stake in a recommendation can still be right. The most tempting trap is (E), because the argument is about an expert, but Brandt doesn't rely on anyone's opinion at all; he dismisses one.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Port Sallow should reject the consultant's conclusion that a seawall is the best protection against storm surges.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Her firm would be hired to design the wall if it were built, so she stands to gain from the recommendation.

breakdown.analysis: So what if she'd profit? Profit gives her a reason to say it, but it doesn't make it false. Brandt never looks at her evidence about surges or seawalls. He just points at her paycheck. It's like ignoring your dentist's advice to fix a cavity because the dentist gets paid for fillings; the cavity is still there. This is ad hominem (the circumstantial kind). It's a classic; know it. Prephrase: attacks the person's motive instead of the recommendation.

choices.note: Cost never comes up. Brandt's only reason is the consultant's stake, so the argument presumes nothing about price.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We should build a seawall rather than restore the dunes, since a seawall is obviously the cheaper choice.

choices.note: So? Whether her firm could profit elsewhere doesn't change what Brandt's argument does wrong. The flaw is dismissing her conclusion because of a motive, not miscounting her motives.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The consultant gains only if a seawall is built, so she has no reason to favor dune restoration, ignoring that her firm might be hired for that too.

choices.note: Brandt doesn't take this for granted; he says nothing about how serious the surges are. And the consultant's claim is about the best protection, which Brandt rejects on other grounds.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We must build a seawall at once, since storm surges are obviously the biggest danger the harbor faces.

choices.note: CORRECT. Brandt's only reason for rejecting the recommendation is the consultant's personal stake in it. That she would gain says nothing about whether a seawall really is the best protection.
Tempting, because the argument is about an expert. But Brandt doesn't rely on anyone's expertise. He rejects an expert's view; he doesn't lean on an off-topic one.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A famous novelist says a seawall is the best defense against storm surges, so the council should build one.

questions.stimulus: Last spring, Hollow Brook Farm installed motorized grooming brushes in its barn, which the cows can use to scratch themselves whenever they like. Over the following six months, the herd's average daily milk yield was 7 percent higher than in the six months before. Clearly, the brushes are responsible for the increase, so the farm should keep them running rather than shut them off to save on electricity.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: draws a general conclusion about all dairy cows from the experience of a single herd on a single farm
fails to consider that the herd's yield might have risen during that period without the brushes
presumes, without providing justification, that saving on electricity is the farm's most important goal
takes for granted that the cows that made use of the brushes enjoyed using them
confuses a condition that is required for a high milk yield with a condition that guarantees one
questions.explanation: Core move: a before/after change treated as proof of cause. The argument compares spring-and-summer yield with the previous autumn-and-winter yield and credits the brushes, without asking whether yield would have risen anyway (season, feed, pasture), which is (B). The most tempting trap is (A), a sampling flaw, but the argument draws no conclusion about dairy cows in general; both claims are about this herd. (C) gets the argument backward: it puts the brushes ahead of electricity savings.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The brushes caused the rise in milk yield, so the farm should keep them running.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brushes went in last spring; average daily yield in the next six months was 7 percent higher than in the previous six.

breakdown.analysis: Is the brush the only thing that changed between those two six-month stretches? Look at the calendar. The 'after' period is spring and summer; the 'before' period is autumn and winter. Fresh pasture, longer days, new calves: lots of things could lift yield. It's like buying a new umbrella in April and crediting it for the sunny weather in June. Prephrase: the argument ignores other causes; yield might have risen anyway.

choices.note: Tempting, because one herd is a small sample. But the argument never generalizes. Both the causal claim and the plan are about this herd only.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our herd gave more milk after we installed brushes, so brushes will raise yield on dairy farms everywhere.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument treats 'yield went up after the brushes' as 'the brushes raised yield.' If yield would have risen over spring and summer anyway, the brushes may have done nothing.
This is backward. The argument explicitly ranks the brushes above the electricity savings. Nothing presumes saving power is the top goal.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We should switch off every machine in the barn at night, since cutting the electric bill matters more than anything else on the farm.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether the cows enjoyed the brushes doesn't matter to the argument, which rests on the yield numbers, and the argument never assumes it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The cows crowd around the brushes, so they must enjoy them, and anything they enjoy must be good for them.

choices.note: There is no conditional here. The argument doesn't say the brushes are required for, or guarantee, high yield; the claim is a simple causal one.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Well-fed cows are needed for a high yield, and our cows are well fed, so our herd will have a high yield.

questions.stimulus: Any singer who passes the Linnet Choral Society's sight-reading audition is guaranteed a place in its chamber choir. Marisol has a place in the chamber choir this season, so she must have passed the sight-reading audition. And since Teodor did not pass that audition, he cannot have a place in the chamber choir.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: treats a requirement for joining the chamber choir as though it were enough to guarantee a place in it
overlooks the possibility that some singers who pass the audition may decline a place in the chamber choir
draws a conclusion about every member of the chamber choir based on only two individual cases
presumes, without providing justification, that the sight-reading audition accurately measures a singer's overall ability
treats a condition that guarantees a place in the chamber choir as though it were required for one
questions.explanation: Core move: sufficient vs. necessary, and noticing which direction the mistake runs. Passing the audition is enough for a place (pass → place), but the argument treats it as required (place → pass, and no pass → no place); there could be other routes in, such as a returning-member invitation. (E) states exactly that error. The most tempting trap is (A), which names the same pair of ideas but reversed: it accuses the argument of treating a requirement as a guarantee, which is the opposite of what it does.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Marisol must have passed the audition, and Teodor, who didn't pass, can't be in the chamber choir.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pass the sight-reading audition → guaranteed a place in the chamber choir.

breakdown.analysis: The rule: pass → place. That tells you passing is one way in. Is it the only way? The argument acts as if it is. Marisol: place → pass. That reverses the arrow. Teodor: no pass → no place. That negates both sides. Both moves only work if passing is required, and the rule never says that. It's like saying anyone who wins the lottery can afford a boat, so your neighbor with a boat must have won the lottery. Prephrase: treats a sufficient condition as a necessary one.

choices.note: Tempting, because it uses the right vocabulary. But it's the reverse error. The premise is a guarantee, and the argument treats it as a requirement, not the other way around.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Only singers who pass the audition can join the chamber choir. Lina passed, so she must have a place in it.

choices.note: So? Someone declining a place would not rescue either conclusion. Marisol has a place, and the question is how she got it; Teodor didn't pass at all.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Every singer who passed the audition was offered a place, so every one of them is singing in the chamber choir this season.

choices.note: The argument draws conclusions only about Marisol and Teodor, not about the whole choir. There's no generalization here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Marisol and Teodor both passed the audition before joining, so every chamber choir member must have passed it.

choices.note: The audition's accuracy doesn't matter. Even a perfect audition would leave open other routes into the choir.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Teodor scored poorly on the sight-reading audition, so he must be a weak singer overall.

choices.note: CORRECT. Passing guarantees a place; it isn't shown to be the only way to get one. The argument treats it as required both ways: every member passed (Marisol), and failing keeps you out (Teodor).

questions.stimulus: Since an automated conveyor system was installed at the Halstow Freight warehouse, some workers have complained that more of them are getting hurt on the job than before. The warehouse's operations manager replies that the complaint is mistaken: in each of the five years before the installation, about 6 percent of the warehouse's workers suffered an on-the-job injury, but last year, the first full year with the conveyors, only 4 percent did.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the manager's reasoning?
choices: It overlooks the possibility that the warehouse employs considerably more workers now than it did before the conveyors were installed.
It fails to consider that last year's injuries may have been more serious, on average, than the injuries in earlier years.
It draws a conclusion about the conveyor system's long-term safety from a single year of injury data.
It presumes, without providing justification, that the conveyor system was responsible for the drop in the injury rate.
It dismisses the workers' complaint on the grounds that the workers have a motive for exaggerating the danger.
questions.explanation: Core move: rate versus number. The workers complained that more of them are getting hurt, a claim about a count, and the manager answers with a percentage; if the warehouse now employs many more workers, 4 percent of the new staff could be more people than 6 percent of the old one, which is what (A) points to without ever naming the rate/number gap. Most students pick (B) because severity is the textbook gap in injury arguments, but the complaint and the rebuttal are both about how many workers were hurt, not how badly, so severity isn't what the manager overlooked. (D) fails because the manager never credits the conveyors with the lower rate; he only says the complaint is false.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The workers' complaint that more of them are getting hurt is mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Before the conveyors, about 6% of workers were injured each year; in the first full year with them, 4% were.

breakdown.analysis: The workers said MORE of them are getting hurt. That's a count. The manager answered with a percentage. Is 4% of the workers fewer people than 6%? Only if the workforce didn't grow. 4% of 500 workers is 20; 6% of 200 is 12. This is the classic rate-versus-number slip; know it. Prephrase: 'ignores that the number of workers may have changed.' The right answer may not use the words 'rate' or 'number' at all; it may just point at a bigger workforce. Most students pick (B), the severity answer, because it's the familiar gap in injury arguments; but nobody here is arguing about how bad the injuries were.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the warehouse hired many more workers (plausible when a big new system goes in), a lower percentage can still mean more injured workers. That's exactly the gap between the manager's rate and the workers' count, described through its cause.

Tempting, and the main trap: severity is a real flaw in many injury arguments. But the complaint is that more workers are getting hurt, and the manager answers about how many. Neither side talks about how badly, so the argument doesn't overlook anything by ignoring severity.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Injuries fell from 30 to 20 last year, so the warehouse is safer now, even though three of last year's injuries were fatal.

choices.note: The manager draws no conclusion about long-term safety. He says only that the complaint about the period since installation is mistaken, and that period is the one year he cites.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Injuries fell in the conveyors' first year, so the conveyors will keep the warehouse safe for decades.

choices.note: The manager never says the conveyors caused the drop. He just uses the rate to deny that injuries rose.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The injury rate fell after the conveyors were installed, so the conveyors must have made the work safer.

choices.note: The manager never mentions the workers' motives. He answers with data.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The workers want a raise, so their complaint about injuries can't be trusted.

questions.stimulus: Meteorologist: Under our agency's standard, a windstorm counts as a derecho only if it produces damaging winds along a path at least 400 kilometers long. Some residents insist that last week's storm was a derecho, and admittedly it was violent: our survey teams confirmed toppled trees and roof damage along a 260-kilometer stretch of the river valley. But the teams confirmed no damage beyond that stretch. So the storm's damage path fell well short of 400 kilometers, and the storm was not a derecho.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the meteorologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: treats a condition required for a storm to be a derecho as though it were sufficient to make a storm one
takes for granted that the survey teams confirmed every instance of damage that the storm caused within the 260-kilometer stretch
presumes, without providing justification, that the survey teams would have confirmed any damage that occurred outside the 260-kilometer stretch
dismisses the residents' view solely on the grounds that the residents lack any professional training or expertise in classifying severe windstorms
overlooks the possibility that some of the damage the teams confirmed was caused by something other than the storm's winds
questions.explanation: Core move: lack of evidence treated as evidence of absence, hidden inside valid conditional logic. The 'only if' rule is used correctly (path under 400 km → not a derecho); the gap is the step from 'the teams confirmed no damage beyond 260 km' to 'there was no damage beyond 260 km,' which works only if the teams would have caught any damage outside the stretch, as (C) says. Most students pick (B), which differs from (C) by one word, 'within': missed damage inside the stretch can't change how long the path was, so the argument doesn't need that presumption. (A) tempts anyone who sees 'only if' and expects a conditional error, but the meteorologist never treats the 400-km condition as sufficient.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Last week's storm was not a derecho.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Derecho → damage path of at least 400 km; teams confirmed damage along 260 km; they confirmed none beyond that; so the path was under 400 km (intermediate conclusion).

breakdown.analysis: First, check the formal logic, because that's where you'll be tempted to pounce. Derecho → 400+ km path. Contrapositive: under 400 km → not a derecho. The meteorologist uses it correctly. So the problem is earlier: how do we know the path was under 400 km? Because the teams 'confirmed no damage beyond that stretch.' Did they even look beyond it? Not finding damage isn't the same as there being none. It's like saying a book has no typos past page 260 because the proofreader found none there, when she may have stopped reading at page 260. Prephrase: the argument takes for granted that the teams would have found any damage beyond the stretch. Most students pick (B), which has the same shape but the wrong location; check the one word that tells you where.

choices.note: Tempting if you see 'only if' and expect the usual error. But the argument uses the rule in its valid contrapositive form: path too short → not a derecho. It never says 400 km is enough to make one.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A storm is a derecho only if its damage path is at least 400 kilometers. This storm's path was 450 kilometers, so it was a derecho.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap: it differs from the right answer by one word, 'within' instead of 'outside.' Missed damage inside the 260 km doesn't change the path's length, so the argument needn't take for granted that the teams caught all of it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The teams found damage at forty sites in the valley, so the storm must have damaged exactly forty sites there.

choices.note: CORRECT. The step from 'no confirmed damage beyond 260 km' to 'the path fell short of 400 km' works only if the teams would have found damage out there had there been any. Without that, the argument treats absence of evidence as evidence of absence.
The meteorologist never mentions the residents' expertise. Their view is rejected on the basis of the survey data, not their credentials.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The residents aren't trained meteorologists, so their claim that the storm was a derecho must be wrong.

choices.note: This would actually help the meteorologist: if some confirmed damage wasn't the storm's, the path is even shorter. A flaw has to be something that leaves the conclusion unsupported.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The storm damaged homes along a 260-kilometer path, so it caused every broken window reported in the valley that week.

questions.stimulus: According to annual counts by the state wildlife agency, the number of young salmon in Pike Creek each spring has doubled since beavers returned to the creek five years ago. Beaver dams create deep, slow pools in which young salmon can shelter from herons and larger fish. So the beavers' return is responsible for the increase in the creek's young salmon.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Before the beavers returned, young salmon in Pike Creek were more exposed to predators than young salmon in other creeks were.
Young salmon in creeks that have no beavers rarely survive long enough to make their own way downstream to the sea.
Beaver dams are the only source of the deep, slow pools in which young salmon in Pike Creek take shelter.
No change in the creek other than the beavers' return is mainly responsible for the increase in young salmon.
The number of young salmon in Pike Creek will keep rising for as long as the beavers remain in the creek.
questions.explanation: Core move: a causal conclusion drawn from a before-and-after change assumes no other change did the work. If some other change, such as cleaner water or reduced fishing, mainly produced the increase, the beavers would not be responsible, so the argument requires (D). The tempting trap is (C): it seems to make the beavers indispensable, but the argument doesn't need them to be the only source of pools; negate it and the beaver pools can still have doubled the salmon. (B) is too strong and is about other creeks.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The beavers' return caused the doubling of young salmon in Pike Creek.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The spring count of young salmon doubled after the beavers returned; beaver dams make pools where young salmon hide from herons and larger fish.

breakdown.analysis: Before and after. But what else changed in five years? Maybe a factory upstream closed, or fishing was banned. When an argument says 'X happened, then Y went up, so X caused Y', it assumes nothing else caused Y. Prephrase: 'Some other change didn't cause the increase.' It's like crediting your new running shoes for a faster mile when you also quit smoking the same month.

choices.note: Irrelevant comparison. Other creeks don't matter. Negate it (salmon here were no more exposed than elsewhere) and beavers could still have doubled them here.
choices.negation: Before the beavers returned, young salmon in Pike Creek were no more exposed to predators than young salmon in other creeks were.

choices.note: Too strong, and about other creeks. Negate it (young salmon in beaver-free creeks often survive) and Pike Creek's beavers could still be the reason for this increase.
choices.negation: Young salmon in creeks that have no beavers do not rarely survive long enough to make their own way downstream to the sea.

choices.note: Tempting: it makes the beavers seem essential. But the argument doesn't need beaver pools to be the only pools. Negate it (there are some other pools too) and the new beaver pools can still explain the doubling.
choices.negation: Beaver dams are not the only source of the deep, slow pools in which young salmon in Pike Creek take shelter.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: some other change is mainly responsible for the increase. Then the beavers aren't responsible, and the argument falls apart.
choices.negation: Some change in the creek other than the beavers' return is mainly responsible for the increase in young salmon.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument explains the past increase; it predicts nothing. Negate it (the numbers will level off) and the conclusion is untouched.
choices.negation: The number of young salmon in Pike Creek will not keep rising for as long as the beavers remain in the creek.

questions.stimulus: Patients who miss appointments at Ridley Hospital's outpatient clinics most often say, when asked, that they simply forgot. The hospital plans to send each patient a reminder through its new mobile app on the day before every appointment, at no cost to the patient. So the plan should substantially reduce the number of missed appointments at the hospital's clinics.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Every patient who forgets an appointment owns a smartphone that is able to run the hospital's new app.
Many of the patients who would otherwise forget their appointments will actually receive the app's reminders.
Reminders sent through the hospital's app will be more effective than reminders sent by ordinary text message.
Patients who miss appointments are no more likely than other patients to have serious health problems.
Forgetting is the only reason that any patient misses an appointment at one of the hospital's outpatient clinics.
questions.explanation: Core move: a plan that works through a channel assumes the channel reaches the people it targets. The reminders can only help patients who get them, so if few forgetful patients use the app, the plan can't substantially reduce missed appointments; that's (B). The tempting trap is (A), which points at the same worry but is too strong: the plan can work even if some forgetful patients lack smartphones. (E) is also too strong, since the stimulus says forgetting is the most common reason, and the plan only needs to cut that one.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The plan to send reminders through the hospital's new app will substantially reduce missed appointments.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Patients who miss appointments most often say they forgot.

breakdown.analysis: Reminders fix forgetting. Fine. But only if the forgetful patients actually get them. A brand-new app: who has it installed? If the forgetful patients mostly don't use it, the reminders go nowhere. Prephrase: 'A good number of the forgetful patients will get the app's reminders.' It's like putting a 'Wet Paint' sign in a room nobody walks into.

choices.note: Tempting: it's the right worry. But 'every' is too strong. Negate it (some forgetful patients don't have a capable phone) and the plan can still reach most of them.
choices.negation: At least one patient who forgets an appointment does not own a smartphone that is able to run the hospital's new app.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: few forgetful patients will receive the reminders. Then the reminders can't make a substantial dent, and the plan fails.
choices.negation: Few of the patients who would otherwise forget their appointments will actually receive the app's reminders.

choices.note: Irrelevant comparison. The plan only needs to work, not to beat text messages. Negate it and the app reminders can still substantially help.
choices.negation: Reminders sent through the hospital's app will not be more effective than reminders sent by ordinary text message.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Health status doesn't affect whether reminders cure forgetting. Negate it and the argument is unaffected.
choices.negation: Patients who miss appointments are more likely than other patients to have serious health problems.

choices.note: Too strong. The stimulus says forgetting is the most common reason, not the only one. Fixing the most common cause can be enough. Negation doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Forgetting is not the only reason that patients miss appointments at the hospital's outpatient clinics.

questions.stimulus: Fuel accounts for 40 percent of the cost of operating the city of Tarnby's fleet of garbage trucks, all of which now run on diesel. The electric garbage trucks that the city is considering buying use no fuel at all. So replacing the city's diesel trucks with electric ones would substantially reduce the cost of operating the fleet.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Electric garbage trucks cost no more to purchase than the diesel garbage trucks the city now uses.
Electric garbage trucks require less maintenance than the diesel garbage trucks that the city currently operates.
The price of diesel fuel in the region is likely to rise steadily over the next several years.
Most cities that have already switched to electric garbage trucks are satisfied with how the trucks perform.
The fleet's other costs, electricity included, would not rise by nearly as much as the fleet saves on fuel.
questions.explanation: Core move: removing a 40 percent slice of a cost only lowers the total if the other slices don't grow to fill the hole. Electric trucks skip fuel but need electricity and may cost more in other ways; if those increases nearly matched the fuel savings, there would be no substantial reduction, so the argument needs (E). The most tempting trap is (A), which raises a real money worry but concerns purchase price, while the conclusion is about operating cost. (B) is also attractive but too strong: maintenance could stay the same and the fuel savings alone would still cut costs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Switching to electric garbage trucks would substantially reduce the fleet's operating cost.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Fuel is 40 percent of operating cost; electric trucks use no fuel.

breakdown.analysis: No fuel. Great. But do electric trucks run on air? Electricity costs money, and maybe batteries or repairs cost more too. Cutting a 40 percent slice only shrinks the pie if the other slices don't swell. Prephrase: 'The new costs won't come close to eating up the fuel savings.' And note the dimension: the conclusion is about operating cost, not purchase price.

choices.note: Tempting: price matters to any city budget. But the conclusion is about operating cost, not buying cost. Negate it (electric trucks cost more to buy) and operating costs could still fall.
choices.negation: Electric garbage trucks cost more to purchase than the diesel garbage trucks the city now uses.

choices.note: Tempting, but too strong. The argument doesn't need maintenance savings. Negate it (maintenance costs the same) and the fuel savings alone still cut the bill.
choices.negation: Electric garbage trucks do not require less maintenance than the diesel garbage trucks that the city currently operates.

choices.note: Strengthens a bit, but isn't required. Negate it (fuel prices stay flat) and fuel is still 40 percent of costs that electric trucks avoid.
choices.negation: The price of diesel fuel in the region is not likely to rise steadily over the next several years.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Other cities' satisfaction isn't Tarnby's operating cost. Negation does nothing to the argument.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most cities that have already switched to electric garbage trucks are satisfied with how the trucks perform.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the fleet's other costs, electricity included, would rise by nearly as much as the fuel savings, or more. Then there's no substantial reduction, and the conclusion fails.
choices.negation: The fleet's other costs, electricity included, would rise by nearly as much as the fleet saves on fuel, or by more.

questions.stimulus: Library board member: Opponents of the self-checkout kiosks installed at the Wexley Public Library last year point out that since then the share of loans going to patrons over sixty-five has fallen from 30 percent to 22 percent. They conclude that the kiosks have discouraged older patrons from borrowing. But the kiosks arrived along with our new children's reading program, which has sharply increased loans to children. So the drop in that share does not show that older patrons are borrowing less.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the board member's argument?
choices: The number of loans to patrons over sixty-five has not declined at all since the self-checkout kiosks were installed.
Patrons over sixty-five find the library's self-checkout kiosks no harder to use than younger adult patrons do.
The increase in loans to children has not been largely offset by a decrease in loans to adult patrons under sixty-five.
Few of the library's patrons over sixty-five take part in the new children's reading program as volunteers.
Before the kiosks were installed, patrons over sixty-five accounted for a larger share of loans than any other age group did.
questions.explanation: Core move: a shrinking share can come from other slices growing, but only if the whole actually grew. The board member blames the drop on the surge in children's loans; if that surge were cancelled out by fewer loans to adults under sixty-five, total loans would be flat, and a fall from 30 to 22 percent would mean older patrons really are borrowing less, so (C) is required. Most students pick (A) because it sounds like the board member's position, but the conclusion is only that the statistic doesn't show a decline; negate (A) to 'loans to older patrons dipped slightly' and the argument about what the numbers show survives. (B) echoes the opponents' story about the kiosks, which the board member's purely numerical rebuttal never touches.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The drop in the over-65 share of loans does not show that older patrons are borrowing less.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The over-65 share fell from 30% to 22%; the kiosks arrived together with a children's program that sharply increased loans to children.

breakdown.analysis: A share is a slice divided by the whole pie. If the pie grows (more children's loans), a slice can shrink as a share without shrinking in size. But what if the pie didn't grow? If adults under 65 borrowed less by about as much as children borrowed more, total loans stay flat, and then a share falling from 30% to 22% means the older patrons' slice really got smaller. So the argument needs the pie to have actually grown. Prephrase: 'the children's surge wasn't cancelled out somewhere else.' Most students pick (A) because it sounds like what the board member believes; but the conclusion is about what the statistic shows, not a claim that older patrons borrow no less.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap: it sounds like the board member's view. But it's too strong. The board member only says the share drop doesn't prove a decline. A small real decline is compatible with that. Negation doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: The number of loans to patrons over sixty-five has declined somewhat since the self-checkout kiosks were installed.

choices.note: This is about the opponents' kiosk story. The board member's rebuttal is purely about the numbers, so negating this leaves it untouched.
choices.negation: Patrons over sixty-five find the library's self-checkout kiosks harder to use than younger adult patrons do.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the children's surge was largely offset by fewer loans to younger adults. Then total loans are roughly flat, and a share falling from 30% to 22% does mean older patrons are borrowing less. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: The increase in loans to children has been largely offset by a decrease in loans to adult patrons under sixty-five.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether older patrons volunteer has nothing to do with whose loans make up the total. Negation doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Many of the library's patrons over sixty-five take part in the new children's reading program as volunteers.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Which group was largest before says nothing about whether the total grew. Negation doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Before the kiosks were installed, patrons over sixty-five did not account for a larger share of loans than every other age group did.

questions.stimulus: Labor economist: Electricians who trained through the Corvane apprenticeship program earn, on average, 20 percent more five years after finishing than electricians who learned the trade in other ways. Some argue that this gap merely reflects the program's practice of admitting only applicants with strong math scores. But the program dropped its math-score requirement fifteen years ago, and the earnings gap is just as large among those admitted since then. So the training the program provides is responsible for much of the gap.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the labor economist's argument depends?
choices: Apprentices admitted since the requirement was dropped have not, on the whole, had math scores as strong as earlier apprentices had.
Apprentices admitted since the requirement was dropped have, on the whole, had weaker math scores than electricians trained in other ways.
Among electricians generally, those with strong math scores do not earn more than those whose math scores are weaker.
No electrician who learned the trade outside the Corvane program earns more than the average graduate of the program.
The Corvane program has not changed what it teaches its apprentices since it dropped its math-score requirement.
questions.explanation: Core move: a rebuttal that leans on a policy change assumes the change actually changed something. The economist answers the selection objection by noting the gap survived the dropped requirement, but if later apprentices still had math scores as strong as earlier ones (say, because only strong students apply), dropping the rule changed nothing and the surviving gap proves nothing; that is (A). Most students pick (B), which differs only in its comparison group: the argument needs later apprentices to be weaker than earlier apprentices, not weaker than outsiders, so negating (B) leaves the argument standing. (C) is too strong, since the economist's point works even if math scores do affect earnings.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The program's training is responsible for much of the 20% earnings gap.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Objection: the gap just reflects admitting strong-math applicants; reply: the math requirement was dropped fifteen years ago, and the gap is just as large among later admits.

breakdown.analysis: Dropping a rule is one thing. Did the people actually change? Maybe the program's reputation still draws only math whizzes, so the class looks the same with or without the rule. Then the gap staying put tells you nothing about training. The reply works only if dropping the rule really did weaken the apprentices' math scores. Prephrase: 'later admits weren't as strong in math as earlier admits.' This is the counterfactual-cause pattern: to credit the training, the alternative cause (selection) has to have actually been removed. Most students pick (B), the same idea with the wrong comparison group; check every comparison word before you commit.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: later admits had math scores just as strong as earlier ones. Then dropping the rule changed nothing, selection could still explain the whole gap, and the rebuttal is empty. The double-negative wording ('have not ... had ... as strong') is the disguise.
choices.negation: Apprentices admitted since the requirement was dropped have, on the whole, had math scores as strong as earlier apprentices had.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap: it's one comparison group away from the right answer. The argument needs later admits to be weaker than earlier admits, not weaker than outsiders. Negate it (later admits are still at least as strong as outsiders) and the argument survives, because their math edge still shrank while the gap held.
choices.negation: Apprentices admitted since the requirement was dropped have not, on the whole, had weaker math scores than electricians trained in other ways.

choices.note: Too strong. The economist doesn't need math to be worthless. Negate it (strong-math electricians do earn more) and the argument stands: the gap held steady even as the program stopped selecting for math.
choices.negation: Among electricians generally, those with strong math scores earn more than those whose math scores are weaker.

choices.note: Way too strong. The comparison is between averages, and a few outsiders can out-earn the average graduate. Negation doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: At least one electrician who learned the trade outside the Corvane program earns more than the average graduate of the program.

choices.note: Not required. If the curriculum changed, the training could still be responsible for the gap. Negation doesn't hurt the conclusion that training matters.
choices.negation: The Corvane program has changed what it teaches its apprentices since it dropped its math-score requirement.

questions.stimulus: This year, every school in the Ashcombe district that hosts a weekly coding club is eligible for a technology grant from the district's education foundation. Millbrook Elementary hosts a weekly coding club. So Millbrook Elementary will be able to replace its aging classroom computers this year.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any school that will be able to replace its aging classroom computers this year is eligible for a technology grant.
Millbrook Elementary's coding club is better attended than the coding club at any other school in the district.
Any school eligible for a technology grant this year will be able to replace its aging classroom computers.
Technology grants awarded to schools in the Ashcombe district may be spent only on classroom computers.
Some schools in the district that do not host a coding club also have aging classroom computers.
questions.explanation: Core move: connect the premise's last term (eligible for a grant) to the conclusion's new term (able to replace computers). Millbrook hosts a club, so it is eligible; (C) says every eligible school will be able to replace its computers, so the conclusion follows. The most tempting trap is (D), which ties the grants to computers, but it only restricts how grant money is spent and never guarantees that an eligible school actually gets a grant or enough money. (A) links the same two terms in the wrong direction.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Millbrook Elementary will be able to replace its aging classroom computers this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Coding club → eligible for a technology grant; Millbrook hosts a coding club.

breakdown.analysis: Millbrook is eligible for a grant. So what? Eligible isn't the same as replacing computers. The argument jumps from one to the other. Chain: coding club → eligible → ??? → can replace computers. We need: eligible → can replace computers. Prephrase: 'Any school eligible for a grant will be able to replace its computers.' New term in the conclusion with no premise behind it? That's your gap.

choices.note: Reversed. This says replacing computers → eligible. We need eligible → replacing computers.
Irrelevant. Popularity doesn't connect eligibility to new computers.
CORRECT. Coding club → eligible → can replace computers. Millbrook goes all the way through.

Tempting, because it puts grants and computers in the same sentence. But it only limits how grant money may be spent. Eligible isn't awarded, and a small grant might not cover the replacement. It doesn't guarantee anything.
Irrelevant. Other schools' computers tell us nothing about Millbrook's.

questions.stimulus: Mayfly larvae in the Sallow River survive only in stretches where the water stays below 20 degrees Celsius throughout the summer. Since the Corran Dam was completed, the stretch of the river just below the dam has no longer stayed that cool in summer. So trout will no longer be able to feed through the summer in that stretch.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the argument's conclusion to be properly drawn?
choices: Trout can feed through the summer in a stretch of the Sallow River only if mayfly larvae survive there.
In any stretch of the Sallow where mayfly larvae survive, trout are able to feed through the summer.
Trout in the Sallow generally prefer to feed in water that is cooler than 20 degrees Celsius.
Before the dam was completed, the stretch just below it supported more mayfly larvae than any other stretch.
Mayfly larvae are the principal food of the trout that live in the Sallow River during the summer.
questions.explanation: Core move: the conclusion introduces trout, so the assumption must tie trout feeding to the premises' mayflies as a necessary condition. The premises establish that mayfly larvae can't survive below the dam; (A) says trout can feed in a stretch only if mayflies survive there, so trout can't feed there. The most tempting trap is (E): if mayflies are the trout's 'principal' food, losing them sounds fatal, but principal isn't exclusive, and trout could feed on other things. (B) gives the reversed, sufficient version of the needed link.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Trout can no longer feed through the summer in the stretch below the dam.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Mayfly larvae survive → water below 20°C all summer; the stretch below the dam no longer stays below 20°C.

breakdown.analysis: So no mayfly larvae below the dam. Fine. But the conclusion is about trout. Why can't trout feed without mayflies? Maybe they eat snails. Chain: not cool → no mayflies → ??? → trout can't feed. We need: no mayflies → trout can't feed, which is the same as trout feed → mayflies survive. Prephrase: 'Trout can feed in a stretch only if mayflies survive there.'

choices.note: CORRECT. Trout feed → mayflies survive. Contrapositive: no mayflies → trout can't feed. The stretch below the dam has no mayflies, so no trout feeding.
Reversed. Mayflies → trout can feed. Below the dam there are no mayflies, so this rule doesn't apply.
A preference isn't a requirement. Trout that prefer cool water can still feed in warmer water.
Irrelevant. How many mayflies the stretch used to have doesn't connect mayflies to trout.
Tempting. It sounds like losing mayflies starves the trout. But 'principal' isn't 'only'. Trout could still feed on whatever else is there. The LSAT is ultra literal: you need a must, not a mostly.

questions.stimulus: A glaze that contains lead can leach it into acidic foods such as tomato sauce or citrus juice, so no glaze that contains lead is food-safe. Every glaze in Kessick Supply's new Heritage line reproduces a nineteenth-century recipe that the company found in old potters' notebooks. Therefore, none of the Heritage glazes is food-safe.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every glaze that is not food-safe contains at least some lead that can leach into acidic foods.
Most of the glaze recipes that potters recorded in the nineteenth century called for some amount of lead.
Some glazes that contain no lead are nonetheless unsafe for use with acidic foods such as citrus juice.
Any glaze made by reproducing a nineteenth-century recipe contains at least some amount of lead.
Kessick Supply markets the Heritage glazes mainly for decorative pieces rather than for tableware.
questions.explanation: Core move: bridge from the term in the premise about the Heritage line (nineteenth-century recipe) to the term in the rule (contains lead).
