With (D), every Heritage glaze reproduces an old recipe, so contains lead, so is not food-safe. The most tempting trap is (B), which points in the right direction but says only 'most', so some Heritage glazes could reproduce lead-free recipes and be food-safe. (A) reverses the lead rule: it says what's true of unsafe glazes, not what's true of leaded ones.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: None of the Heritage glazes is food-safe.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Contains lead → not food-safe; every Heritage glaze reproduces a nineteenth-century recipe from old potters' notebooks.

breakdown.analysis: Old recipe. So what? Who says old recipes contain lead? That's the missing link. Chain: Heritage → 19th-century recipe → ??? → contains lead → not food-safe. Prephrase: 'Every glaze made from a nineteenth-century recipe contains lead.' Since the conclusion says 'none', the link has to cover every Heritage glaze, so it needs 'every', not 'most'.

choices.note: Reversed. Not food-safe → lead. We need lead on the other side: old recipe → lead → not food-safe. This rule never gets us from Heritage to unsafe.
Tempting: it's the right idea. But 'most' isn't enough for 'none of the Heritage glazes'. Some Heritage glazes could copy the lead-free minority of old recipes and be perfectly food-safe.
So? Other reasons a glaze might be unsafe don't show that the Heritage glazes have any of them.
CORRECT. Heritage → 19th-century recipe → contains lead → not food-safe. Every Heritage glaze makes the trip. 'At least some lead' is all the rule needs: any lead at all means not food-safe.
Irrelevant. How Kessick markets the glazes doesn't change whether they are food-safe.

questions.stimulus: Town treasurer: Our charter permits money to be drawn from the reserve fund only for expenses that were unforeseeable when the year's budget was adopted. Last winter the Dell Street library's roof collapsed under heavy snow and must be replaced. Admittedly, nobody predicted a collapse. But an engineer's report completed months before this year's budget was adopted documented the badly deteriorated condition that caused the collapse. So the replacement cannot properly be paid for from the reserve fund.
questions.stem: The treasurer's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any expense that was unforeseeable when the year's budget was adopted may properly be paid for from the reserve fund.
The members of the town council read the engineer's report before they voted to adopt this year's budget.
An expense that nobody actually predicted can nonetheless have been foreseeable at the time a budget was adopted.
The roof would not have collapsed last winter if it had been repaired soon after the engineer's report was completed.
An expense that results from a condition documented before a budget was adopted was not unforeseeable when that budget was adopted.
questions.explanation: Core move: the charter states a necessary condition (reserve money → unforeseeable expense), so the treasurer must show this expense was not unforeseeable, and only (E) gets there, in deliberately double-negative wording. The deterioration that caused the collapse was documented before the budget, so by (E) the replacement was not unforeseeable, and by the charter's contrapositive the reserve can't pay for it. Most students pick (C) because it answers the concession that 'nobody predicted a collapse,' but it says only that such an expense can have been foreseeable, not that this one was, so the conclusion still doesn't follow. (A) reverses the charter and could only ever permit reserve spending.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The roof replacement cannot properly be paid for from the reserve fund.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Reserve money → expense unforeseeable when the budget was adopted; nobody predicted the collapse (concession); but the deterioration that caused it was documented in a report before the budget was adopted.

breakdown.analysis: Documented in a report, sure. But does a report sitting in a file make the expense 'foreseeable' under the charter? The argument never says. The charter gives reserve → unforeseeable; contrapositive: not unforeseeable → no reserve money. So we need a bridge from 'cause documented before the budget' to 'not unforeseeable.' Chain: documented cause → not unforeseeable → no reserve money. Most students pick (C) because the 'Admittedly, nobody predicted' line looks like the weak spot, and (C) addresses it. It fails because 'can have been' is only a possibility, and a sufficient assumption has to force the conclusion.

choices.note: This reverses the charter. The charter says reserve → unforeseeable; this says unforeseeable → may be paid. It can only ever permit reserve spending, never forbid it.
So? Council members reading the report makes foresight more plausible, but no rule says reading a report makes an expense 'not unforeseeable.' The conclusion still doesn't follow.

Tempting, because it answers the concession head-on. But 'can have been foreseeable' only removes an objection; it never says this expense was foreseeable. Possibility isn't enough for a sufficient assumption.
Irrelevant to the charter. Whether a repair would have prevented the collapse says nothing about whether the expense was foreseeable when the budget passed.

CORRECT. The collapse came from a condition documented before the budget, so the replacement was not unforeseeable. Charter contrapositive: not unforeseeable → no reserve money. The conclusion follows.

questions.stimulus: Birding club president: Under our bylaws, only members who have submitted sighting logs in each of the past three seasons may vote in the officers' election. Some members object that this rule shuts out the club's newest birders, and that is true. But it does not shut out our dues-paying members: every member who has submitted logs in each of the past three seasons has also paid this year's dues. Hence, at least some of this year's dues-paying members may vote in the election.
questions.stem: The president's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every member who has paid this year's dues has submitted sighting logs in each of the past three seasons.
At least one member of the club is permitted to vote in this year's election of the club's officers.
Any member who has submitted sighting logs in each of the past three seasons may vote in the election of club officers.
Some members who have submitted sighting logs in each of the past three seasons have paid this year's dues.
None of the club's newest birders has paid this year's dues to the club's treasurer.
questions.explanation: Core move: a 'some' conclusion needs at least one person to exist, and nothing in the premises says anyone may vote. The rules give vote → logs every season → dues paid, so any eligible voter is a dues-paying member; (B) supplies one eligible voter, and that person is the dues-paying voter the conclusion needs. Most students pick (C) because it seems to turn the bylaw's 'only' into the missing link, but even if every three-season logger may vote, nothing says any member has actually logged all three seasons, so the group of voters could be empty. (D) has the same existence problem plus a direction problem, since logging is only required for voting.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: At least some of this year's dues-paying members may vote in the election.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: May vote → logs in each of the past three seasons; logs in each season → paid this year's dues; (concession: the rule shuts out the newest birders).

breakdown.analysis: Chain: may vote → logs all three seasons → paid dues. So every voter pays dues. Fine. But is there any voter at all? Every premise is an 'if'; none says anybody exists. 'All dragons breathe fire' doesn't prove that some fire-breather is a dragon. The conclusion is a 'some' claim, so we need existence. Prephrase: 'Someone may vote.' That looks too trivial to be the answer, which is exactly how it hides. Most students pick (C) because it upgrades 'only' to 'any' and looks like a bridge; it fails because a conditional with nobody in it proves nothing about 'some.'

choices.note: This reverses the second premise (dues → logs instead of logs → dues), and it still doesn't say anyone may vote.

CORRECT. One eligible voter exists. Voter → logs → paid dues, so that person is a dues-paying member who may vote, and 'at least some' is proven. The answer looks almost too obvious to matter; that's the disguise.

Tempting, and the main trap. It flips 'only' into 'any,' which feels like the missing link. But it's still a conditional: if nobody has logged all three seasons, nobody may vote and the conclusion fails.

Logs are necessary for voting, not sufficient, so these dues-paying loggers might still be barred from voting. It also adds nothing new: the premises already say every three-season logger has paid dues.
This is about the newest birders, whom the president already concedes are shut out. It says nothing about whether any dues-payer may vote.

questions.stimulus: This season the director of the Halden Community Choir began leading a ten-minute vocal warm-up at the start of every rehearsal. Singers reported hoarseness after rehearsals far less often this season than they had last season. The director concludes that the warm-up reduced hoarseness among the singers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's argument?
choices: Several singers in the choir said that they enjoyed the warm-up and hoped the director would continue it next season.
Singers who missed this season's warm-ups reported hoarseness about as often as the choir did last season.
Last season, the choir did not do any vocal warm-up at the start of its rehearsals or at any other time.
Hoarseness after singing can be caused by a cold or other illness as well as by strain on the voice.
The choir added several new members at the start of this season, and a few longtime members left.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen a causal claim by showing the effect tracks the cause. If this season's singers who missed the warm-up were as hoarse as the choir was last season, the drop shows up only among those who warmed up, which is what (B) says. The most tempting trap is (C): it sounds supportive, but it only restates what 'began leading a warm-up' already implies and adds no new reason to credit the warm-up. (D) and (E) raise side issues without linking the warm-up to the change.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new warm-up reduced hoarseness among the singers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The warm-up began this season; reports of hoarseness after rehearsals fell sharply compared with last season.

breakdown.analysis: Hoarseness dropped after the warm-up started. But a lot can change between seasons: easier music, shorter rehearsals, a milder winter. How would we know it's the warm-up? Look at the singers who didn't get it. If they're still hoarse, the warm-up is the difference. It's like testing a new sunscreen: the best evidence is that the people who skipped it still got burned. Prephrase: those who missed the warm-up didn't improve.

choices.note: So? Enjoying the warm-up, or wanting more of it, doesn't mean it reduced hoarseness.
CORRECT. Same season, same music, same rehearsals, but no warm-up, and no improvement. That isolates the warm-up as the difference.

Tempting, because it fits the director's story. But the stimulus already says the warm-up began this season, so this just repeats a premise. It adds no new reason to credit the warm-up over easier music, shorter rehearsals or a milder winter.
Irrelevant on its own. Knowing hoarseness has several causes doesn't tell us whether the warm-up caused this drop. If anything, it hints at other explanations.
So? Some singers came and some went; that could push hoarseness up or down. It doesn't link the warm-up to the decline.

questions.stimulus: Last year the Kesterton distribution warehouse replaced its dim overhead lights with much brighter LED fixtures. In the six months after the change, the number of orders shipped with the wrong item fell by 25 percent compared with the six months before, even though the warehouse shipped about the same number of orders. The manager concludes that the brighter lighting reduced picking errors.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the manager's argument?
choices: The new LED fixtures use far less electricity than the old overhead lights did and need replacing less often.
Picking errors at Kesterton had been declining steadily for several years before the new lights were installed.
Most of the warehouse's pickers said in a survey that they prefer the new lights to the old.
Picking errors did not decline over the same period at the company's other warehouses, where the lighting was left unchanged.
Shipping the wrong item costs the company more, on average, than any other kind of shipping error does.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen with a comparison group that rules out a general cause. If similar warehouses that kept their old lights saw no decline, a company-wide change (new software, training, products) is unlikely to explain Kesterton's drop, which points to the lighting, as (D) says. The most tempting trap is (C): workers liking the light feels like support, but a preference isn't evidence that errors fell because of the light. (B) actually weakens, since a pre-existing downward trend offers another explanation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The brighter lighting reduced picking errors at Kesterton.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lights were replaced; wrong-item shipments fell 25 percent over the next six months with about the same order volume.

breakdown.analysis: Errors fell after the new lights. Volume is held steady, so it isn't just fewer orders. But what about everything else the company might have changed, like new scanners, new training, a new product line? We want evidence that without the lights, errors wouldn't have fallen. It's like a student who switched desks and got better grades; you'd want to know whether everyone's grades rose that term. Prephrase: places without the new lights saw no improvement.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Saving electricity says nothing about picking errors.
This weakens. If errors were already falling for years, the drop might be the same trend continuing, with or without the lights.
Tempting, because happy workers seem to fit the story. But liking the lights doesn't show the lights reduced errors. Preference isn't performance.
CORRECT. The company's other warehouses, without new lights, saw no decline. That makes a company-wide cause unlikely and points to what was different at Kesterton: the lighting.
Irrelevant. This tells us the errors are costly, not what reduced them.

questions.stimulus: Each summer, the Tarrow County weather office estimates the county's rainfall using readings from rain gauges maintained by volunteers. This summer, the volunteers' gauges recorded, on average, 31 percent less rain than their own long-term summer averages. The office concludes that the county as a whole received substantially less rain than usual this summer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the weather office's argument?
choices: The volunteers' gauges are distributed throughout the county, including the normally wetter hill district.
Most of the volunteers have recorded rainfall at the same location for more than ten years.
A few of the volunteers' gauges recorded more rain this summer than their own long-term summer averages.
Lower-than-usual summer rainfall can significantly reduce the yields of several of the county's most important crops.
There are more volunteer gauges in the county this summer than there were ten years ago.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen a generalization by showing the sample represents the whole. The gauges speak for the county only if they cover the county; if they were clustered in one dry pocket, the hill district could have had a normal summer, so (A), which says they cover all parts, including the wetter hills, shores up the inference. The most tempting trap is (E): more gauges sounds like a better sample, but a larger sample can still be bunched in one area, and size is not coverage. (B) is the other serious contender, but long service supports the reliability of each gauge's average, not whether the gauges together represent the county.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The county as a whole received substantially less rain than usual this summer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Volunteer gauges recorded, on average, 31 percent less rain than their own long-term averages.

breakdown.analysis: The gauges were dry. Was the county? That depends on where the gauges are. Volunteers put gauges where they live, maybe all in the lowland towns. Summer storms can be patchy; the hills could have been soaked while the towns stayed dry. It's like judging a whole city's traffic from cameras on one street. Prephrase: the gauges are spread across the whole county.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the gauges are spread throughout the county, including the wetter hills, their combined shortfall is a fair picture of the county as a whole.
Tempting, because it makes each gauge's long-term average more trustworthy. But reliable gauges in the wrong places still miss the rest of the county. This is about accuracy, not coverage.
This is expected with any average and doesn't help. If anything it hints that some places had a wet summer.
Irrelevant. This is a consequence of low rain, not evidence that the county had low rain.
Tempting, because bigger samples sound better. But more gauges can still sit in the same few towns. Size isn't representativeness, and the comparison is each gauge against its own average anyway.

questions.stimulus: Coastal geologist: Since the town of Wexmouth built an offshore breakwater five years ago, its main beach has lost far less sand each year than it did in the decade before. Some residents attribute the change to the unusually mild storm seasons of the past five years. But storms, though less frequent, have not been absent. I conclude that the breakwater is largely responsible for the reduction in sand loss.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the geologist's argument?
choices: Several strong storms struck the Wexmouth coast during the past five years, though fewer than in the decade before that.
Most of the sand Wexmouth's beach lost before the breakwater was built was carried off during a handful of severe storms.
The breakwater cost Wexmouth considerably less to build than its engineers had projected when it was first proposed.
Some of the residents who credit the mild storm seasons for the change had opposed building the breakwater in the first place.
A nearby beach without a breakwater, exposed to the same storms, has continued to lose sand at its usual rate.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen a causal claim by defeating the rival explanation, not by echoing a premise. The geologist's own reply is weak, since 'storms have not been absent' doesn't show the milder seasons didn't matter; (E) supplies a nearby beach that faced the same mild weather without a breakwater and kept losing sand at its usual rate, so mild weather alone can't explain Wexmouth's change. Most students pick (A) because it confirms the geologist's premise that storms still came; but it also grants that storms were fewer than before, which is the residents' whole point, so it adds nothing the argument didn't already have. (B) actually helps the residents.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The breakwater is largely responsible for the reduced sand loss.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Sand loss dropped after the breakwater was built; residents blame mild storm seasons; reply: storms, though less frequent, haven't been absent.

breakdown.analysis: Storms 'have not been absent.' So what? Fewer storms could still explain less sand loss. The geologist's rebuttal doesn't actually rule out the residents' story. To strengthen, we need something that separates the breakwater from the weather. Best tool: a comparison case. Same weather, no breakwater: if that beach kept losing sand, the weather isn't doing the work. Most students pick (A), because it agrees with the geologist's premise. That's irrelevant corroboration: confirming a premise you already have doesn't fix the gap.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap: it backs up the geologist's own premise. But it also concedes that storms were fewer than before, which is all the residents need. Repeating a premise doesn't close the gap.
This hurts. If most past loss came from a few severe storms, then a stretch with fewer storms would explain the drop without any breakwater.
Cost is irrelevant to what caused the reduction in sand loss.
Attacks the residents' motives, not their explanation. Opponents of a project can still be right about what caused a change.

CORRECT. A beach with the same mild weather and no breakwater kept losing sand at its usual rate. So mild weather alone doesn't cut sand loss, and the breakwater becomes the best explanation for Wexmouth's change.

questions.stimulus: Perfumer: After our house replaced the natural oakmoss extract in its fragrance Calder with a synthetic substitute, customer reports of skin irritation fell from about 1 per 2,000 bottles sold to about 1 per 9,000. A rival claims this merely reflects a change in who buys Calder, since the reformulated scent appeals to a younger clientele. But younger skin is, if anything, more prone to irritation than older skin. So the synthetic substitute is what reduced irritation.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the perfumer's argument?
choices: Younger customers who get skin irritation from a fragrance are less likely than older customers to report it.
Calder's sales have risen since the reformulation, mainly because of new purchases by customers under thirty.
Customers in every age group who get skin irritation from a fragrance are about equally likely to report it.
Some synthetic substitutes for natural fragrance ingredients can themselves cause skin irritation in a small number of users.
The synthetic substitute costs the house less per bottle than the natural oakmoss extract did, and lasts longer.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the gap the rebuttal left open. The perfumer answers the rival with a fact about how often skin gets irritated, but the evidence is about how often irritation is reported; a younger clientele that reports less would cut reports without any real change in irritation, and (C) closes that gap by making reporting independent of age. Most students pick (A) because it is about exactly the right issue, reporting by age; but it runs the wrong way: if younger customers report less, the new clientele could explain the drop in reports, which weakens the perfumer. (B) only confirms the rival's premise that the clientele got younger.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The synthetic substitute is what reduced skin irritation.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Irritation reports fell from 1 per 2,000 bottles to 1 per 9,000; rival: the buyers got younger; reply: younger skin is, if anything, more prone to irritation.

breakdown.analysis: Look at what was measured: reports, not irritation. The perfumer's reply is about skin. But what if younger customers just don't bother to complain? Then a younger clientele could cut reports even while irritating more skin. The rebuttal doesn't cover that. Prephrase: 'younger customers report irritation at least as readily as older ones.' Most students pick (A), because it's about the very same issue. Read the direction: 'less likely to report' opens the gap instead of closing it.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap: it's about reporting by age, the exact issue. But it points the wrong way. If younger buyers report less, the younger clientele could explain the drop in reports. This weakens.
This confirms the rival's premise that the buyers got younger. It doesn't help the perfumer at all.

CORRECT. If reporting doesn't vary with age, reports track actual irritation. Then a shift to younger, more irritation-prone buyers should have raised reports. Since reports fell, the substitute gets the credit.
This mildly hurts: if synthetics can irritate too, it's less clear why switching would help. Either way it doesn't support the perfumer.
Cost and longevity have nothing to do with irritation.

questions.stimulus: In March, the perfume maker Sorrel & Vine began airing radio advertisements for its fragrance Juniper Hour, which it had never before advertised on radio. Sales of Juniper Hour in April were 30 percent higher than in February. The company's marketing director concluded that the radio advertisements were responsible for the increase.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the marketing director's argument?
choices: The radio advertisements cost more to produce than any other advertising that the company had previously done.
Some customers who bought Juniper Hour in April said that they had never heard any of the radio advertisements.
Starting in March, Juniper Hour was also sold in a large national chain of department stores for the first time.
Juniper Hour is more expensive than most of the other fragrances that Sorrel & Vine has ever sold.
Sales of Juniper Hour rose again in May, after the radio advertisements had been running for two full months.
questions.explanation: Core move: weaken a causal claim by supplying another cause that changed at the same time. If Juniper Hour reached a big department store chain in the very month the ads started, that alone could explain the sales jump, as (C) says. The most tempting trap is (B): it sounds like evidence against the ads, but a few buyers who missed the ads tell us nothing about whether the ads drove the increase, since some sales happen without any advertising. (E) if anything supports the director.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The radio advertisements caused the rise in Juniper Hour sales.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The ads began in March; April sales were 30 percent higher than February sales.

breakdown.analysis: Sales went up after the ads started. Did anything else change in March? The director assumes the ads are the only explanation. To weaken, we want a different reason sales would jump right then. It's like getting a raise the same week you start wearing a lucky tie, and crediting the tie. Prephrase: something else that happened around March boosted sales.

choices.note: Irrelevant. What the ads cost says nothing about whether they caused the sales increase.

Tempting, because it seems to show the ads didn't reach everyone. But 'some' buyers is expected: people bought Juniper Hour before any ads existed. The question is what caused the extra 30 percent, and this doesn't touch that.
CORRECT. A large new set of stores selling the fragrance, starting the same month as the ads, is a strong alternative cause. The increase could come from wider availability, not the ads.
So? Price doesn't explain why sales rose between February and April, and it doesn't separate the ads from any other cause.
This leans the other way. Continued growth while the ads keep running fits the director's view, so it can't weaken it.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago the coastal town of Gullhaven banned bonfires on its beaches after dark. Since then, the number of sea turtle nests found on Gullhaven's beaches each summer has nearly doubled. Town officials conclude that the light from beach bonfires had been discouraging sea turtles from nesting there, and they credit the ban for the increase.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the officials' argument?
choices: Sea turtles are known to avoid nesting on beaches that are brightly lit at night by fires or buildings.
Several residents of Gullhaven have been fined for lighting bonfires on the beaches since the ban took effect.
The ban on beach bonfires was opposed by many of Gullhaven's business owners when it was first proposed.
Gullhaven's beaches are longer than the beaches of most of the neighboring towns along the coast.
Nest counts also nearly doubled over those two years on nearby beaches where bonfires have always been allowed.
questions.explanation: Core move: use a comparison group to show the change would have happened anyway. If nests nearly doubled on nearby beaches that still allow bonfires, the rise at Gullhaven is likely part of a regional trend rather than an effect of the ban, which is (E). The most tempting trap is (B): it suggests the ban was not fully obeyed, but a handful of fines doesn't mean bonfires stayed common, and the ban could still have cut them sharply. (A) strengthens the officials' view.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Bonfire light had been discouraging sea turtles from nesting on Gullhaven's beaches.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Bonfires were banned two years ago; nests have nearly doubled since then.

breakdown.analysis: Nests went up after the ban. But would they have gone up anyway? We have no comparison. If turtles were nesting more all along the coast, the ban gets credit it didn't earn. It's like a school crediting its new reading program when every school in the state saw the same score jump. Prephrase: show that nests rose just as much where nothing changed.

choices.note: This strengthens. If turtles avoid lit beaches, removing bonfire light should help, which is just what the officials claim.
Tempting, because it hints the ban wasn't obeyed. But a few fines don't show bonfires stayed common. The ban could still have removed most of them, so the officials' explanation survives.
Irrelevant. Business owners' opinions about the ban have nothing to do with why turtles nest.
So? Beach length was the same before and after the ban, so it can't explain the change.

CORRECT. Beaches that kept their bonfires saw the same near-doubling over the same two years. That points to something affecting the whole coast, such as more turtles in the area, rather than the ban.

questions.stimulus: Over the past five years, about a third of the restaurants in the Brackley district have replaced their gas ranges with induction cooktops, which heat pans without an open flame. Last year, 8 percent of cooks at the switched restaurants suffered a burn requiring medical treatment, compared with 15 percent of cooks at restaurants that kept their gas ranges. A safety inspector concludes that induction cooktops reduce cooks' risk of serious burns.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the inspector's argument?
choices: Before switching, the restaurants that adopted induction cooktops already had much lower burn rates than the others.
Induction cooktops cost considerably more to purchase and install than gas ranges of comparable size do.
Serious burns are much more common among cooks with little experience than among cooks with many years of experience.
Fewer cooks in total work at the switched restaurants than at the restaurants that kept their gas ranges.
Some of the restaurants that switched to induction cooktops did so mainly in order to reduce their energy costs.
questions.explanation: Core move: show that the two groups differed before the supposed cause. If the switched restaurants already had much lower burn rates before they changed equipment, last year's gap reflects the restaurants, not the cooktops, which is (A). The most tempting trap is (C): it names a real alternative cause (inexperience), but it never says the gas-range kitchens have less experienced cooks, so it weakens only if you add an assumption. (D) is a numbers trap; the argument compares rates, so the total number of cooks in each group doesn't matter.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Induction cooktops reduce cooks' risk of serious burns.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last year, 8 percent of cooks at restaurants that switched to induction suffered a burn needing treatment vs. 15 percent at restaurants that kept gas.

breakdown.analysis: Two groups, two rates, one difference credited to the cooktops. But the restaurants chose to switch; they weren't assigned. Were they already different? If those kitchens always had fewer burns (better training, calmer service, more staff), the gap was there before anyone touched an induction cooktop. It's like noting that students who chose an elective have higher grades and crediting the elective, when they were already the top students. Prephrase: the switched restaurants differed from the others in burn rates before the switch.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the switched restaurants already had much lower burn rates before changing equipment, last year's 8 vs. 15 percent gap could be entirely pre-existing. The cooktops get no credit.
Wrong dimension. Cost isn't safety. This might matter to an owner deciding whether to switch, but not to whether induction lowers burns.

Tempting, because experience is a plausible alternative cause. But nothing says the gas-range kitchens have less experienced cooks. You'd have to assume that, and you can't pick an answer on a possibility.
A numbers trap. The comparison is in percentages, so the size of each group doesn't change the rates being compared.
So? Why an owner switched doesn't affect what the switch did to the cooks' burn risk.

questions.stimulus: Highway engineer: Twelve years ago our department repainted eighteen of its steel bridges, all in the same summer and by the same crew. Nine received a new zinc-rich coating; the other nine received the conventional coating we had always used. Inspections this year found that the bridges with the new coating had, on average, less than half as much corrosion as the others. So the new coating protects steel from corrosion far better than the conventional coating does.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the engineer's argument?
choices: The crew that applied both coatings had never before worked with a zinc-rich coating, though it had applied the conventional one many times.
On steel bridges, corrosion generally spreads faster during the second decade after painting than it does during the first.
The new zinc-rich coating costs considerably more to apply than the conventional coating that the department has always used.
The nine bridges given the new coating are all in the hill district, where little road salt is used in winter.
The conventional coating has adequately protected the department's steel bridges from corrosion for many decades.
questions.explanation: Core move: weaken a comparison by finding another difference between the groups that could produce the result. The engineer controls for timing and crew, but (D) reveals that every new-coating bridge sits where little road salt is used, and road salt speeds corrosion, so the coating may deserve none of the credit. Most students pick (A) because it seems to expose a workmanship problem the engineer missed; but a crew unfamiliar with the new coating would, if anything, have applied it worse, which makes the new coating's better showing more impressive, not less. (B) affects both groups alike, since all eighteen bridges were painted the same summer.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new coating protects steel from corrosion far better than the conventional coating.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Eighteen bridges painted the same summer by the same crew; nine got the new coating, nine the old; this year the new-coating bridges had less than half the corrosion.

breakdown.analysis: The engineer did a decent job: same summer, same crew. But were the bridges themselves alike? What if the new-coating bridges just live an easier life? Prephrase: some difference between the two groups of bridges, other than the coating, that could explain less corrosion. It's like crediting a new tire brand for lasting longer when every car with those tires was driven only on dry roads. Most students pick (A) because 'the crew didn't know the new coating' sounds like a workmanship confound. Check its direction: a clumsy application would hurt the new coating, so a strong result despite it helps the engineer.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It sounds like a hidden difference in workmanship. But the inexperience cuts against the new coating, so if the new coating still won by a mile, the argument looks stronger. Directionally wrong.
All eighteen bridges were painted the same summer, so all are in their second decade together. A general speed-up hits both groups alike.
Wrong dimension. Cost says nothing about how well the coating protects steel.

CORRECT. Road salt speeds corrosion. If every new-coating bridge sits where little salt is used, their lower corrosion could come from the location, not the coating. That's an alternative cause the engineer didn't control for.
So? The old coating can be adequate and the new one still far better. This doesn't touch the comparison.

questions.stimulus: Education consultant: Three years ago every high school in Marlow began a peer tutoring program in which strong math students coach struggling ones, and within two years the share of Marlow students failing ninth-grade algebra fell from 21 percent to 14 percent. Rennick's high schools resemble Marlow's in size and in students' prior math scores. Admittedly, Rennick's teachers are less experienced than Marlow's, but the program depends on student tutors, not teachers. So Rennick can expect a similar decline if it adopts the program.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the consultant's argument?
choices: Rennick's mathematics teachers have, on average, fewer than half as many years of classroom experience as do the mathematics teachers in Marlow.
When its program began, Marlow also began placing students who had failed eighth-grade math in a remedial course instead of algebra.
Rennick's current failure rate in ninth-grade algebra is slightly lower than the rate that Marlow had before its program began.
Some cities that adopted peer tutoring programs later abandoned them because of difficulties in scheduling tutoring sessions after school.
Many of Marlow's student tutors reported that coaching struggling classmates had improved their own grasp of algebra as well.
questions.explanation: Core move: attack the evidence the analogy rests on rather than the analogy itself. The consultant labors over whether Rennick resembles Marlow, but (B) shows that Marlow's drop may not have come from tutoring at all: moving the students most likely to fail out of ninth-grade algebra would cut the failure rate by itself, leaving no tutoring effect to transfer. Most students pick (A) because the teacher gap is the one difference the stimulus flags; but the consultant already concedes that Rennick's teachers are less experienced and argues that the program runs on student tutors, and (A) only enlarges the conceded gap without touching that reply. (C) still leaves plenty of room for a similar decline.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Rennick can expect a similar drop in algebra failures if it adopts Marlow's peer tutoring program.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Marlow's failure share fell from 21% to 14% after the program began; Rennick resembles Marlow in size and prior scores; (concession) Rennick's teachers are less experienced, but the program depends on student tutors.

breakdown.analysis: The consultant works hard on one question: is Rennick like Marlow? But there's an earlier question nobody asked: did tutoring actually cause Marlow's drop? If something else happened in Marlow at the same time, there's no tutoring effect to copy, however similar the towns are. Prephrase: another reason Marlow's failure rate fell. It's like copying a neighbor's diet because he lost weight, without noticing he also started running. Most students pick (A) because the stimulus waves the teacher difference in front of you. But the consultant already granted it and answered it; a bigger version of a conceded point doesn't touch the reply.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It attacks the one difference the stimulus flags. But the consultant has already conceded that Rennick's teachers are less experienced and argued that the program runs on student tutors. Making the gap bigger doesn't answer that reply.

CORRECT. If the students most likely to fail stopped taking ninth-grade algebra the year the program began, the failure rate would drop with no help from tutoring. Then Marlow's numbers give Rennick no reason to expect anything from the program.
A slightly lower starting rate still leaves plenty of room for a decline like Marlow's. This barely touches the prediction.
Other cities' scheduling troubles are outside the argument. Nothing says Rennick would face them, and the claim is about what happens if Rennick adopts the program.
This, if anything, helps: it describes a benefit of tutoring. It doesn't suggest the program failed to cause Marlow's decline.

questions.stimulus: Last year the number of passengers flying out of Dunmore Regional Airport rose by nearly 15 percent, and the airport's busiest month set a new record. Over the same period, however, the number of flights departing from the airport fell by about a tenth, and no new airline began service there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Several other airports within a two-hour drive of Dunmore also reported increases in passenger numbers last year.
The average price of a ticket on flights departing from Dunmore rose slightly last year.
Last year Dunmore's airlines replaced many of their small planes with larger ones that carry far more passengers each.
Last year two of the airlines that had offered flights from Dunmore ended their service at the airport.
Most passengers who flew out of Dunmore last year were traveling for business rather than for leisure.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the one fact that lets both halves be true at once. More passengers on fewer flights is no puzzle if each flight carries more people, and C says the airlines switched to much larger planes. The most tempting trap is D, because it explains why there were fewer flights; but it does nothing to explain how passenger numbers rose anyway, so it resolves only half the puzzle. A is about other airports, and B, if anything, makes the passenger increase harder to explain.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Passengers flying out of Dunmore rose almost 15 percent, but departing flights fell about 10 percent.

breakdown.analysis: How can more people fly on fewer flights? Easy: each flight has to carry more people. That means bigger planes or fuller planes. We need an answer that says the average flight held more passengers. It's like a bus company that runs fewer buses but switches to double-deckers: fewer trips, more riders.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Other airports growing tells us nothing about how Dunmore fit more passengers onto fewer flights.
So? Higher prices would, if anything, push passenger numbers down. That makes the rise harder to explain, not easier.
CORRECT. Bigger planes mean more seats per flight. Fewer flights times more seats per flight can easily equal more passengers. Both facts now fit.

Tempting. This explains the drop in flights. But the puzzle has two halves, and this leaves the other one standing: losing two airlines should cut passengers, not raise them. A half-explanation isn't a resolution.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. Why people travel doesn't tell us how more of them fit on fewer flights.

questions.stimulus: At the Fenwick Wildlife Rehabilitation Center, injured owls that receive daily physical therapy are less likely to be successfully released back into the wild than are injured owls that receive no therapy at all. Nevertheless, the center’s veterinarians are confident that the therapy improves an injured owl’s chances of being released.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Owls that are successfully released from the center are rarely brought back to it with new injuries.
Daily handling during therapy can make some owls less wary of people, a trait that endangers them after release.
The center treats more injured owls each year than does any other rehabilitation facility in the region.
Veterinarians at most other wildlife rehabilitation centers also recommend physical therapy for injured owls.
The center gives daily therapy only to owls whose injuries are too severe to heal without it.
questions.explanation: Core move: notice that the two groups being compared may not start out alike. If therapy goes only to the owls with the worst injuries (E), those owls would be released less often even if therapy helps each of them, so the vets' confidence and the lower release rate are compatible. The most tempting trap is B, because it explains why therapy owls are released less often; but it does so by saying therapy hurts, which makes the veterinarians' confidence harder to understand rather than easier. D just adds more people who share the vets' view, and A and C don't touch the comparison.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Owls that get daily therapy are released less often than owls that get none, yet the vets are confident the therapy improves an owl's chances of release.

breakdown.analysis: If therapy helps, why do therapy owls do worse? Ask who gets therapy. If the center gives therapy to the most badly hurt owls, those owls start out far behind. Therapy could lift them a lot and they'd still trail the owls with minor injuries. We need an answer that says the therapy group started out worse off. It's like noticing that hospital patients who get surgery die more often than patients who get a bandage. The surgery isn't the problem; the surgery patients were sicker.

choices.note: Irrelevant. What happens after a successful release doesn't explain why therapy owls are released less often in the first place.

Tempting. This does explain why therapy owls are released less often. But it explains it by saying the therapy hurts them. Then why are the vets confident it helps? This answer resolves one side by making the other side worse.
So? The center's size tells us nothing about the difference between the two groups of owls.
This just says more vets agree. Agreement isn't an explanation. The puzzle is how the vets can be right given the release numbers, and this doesn't touch that.

CORRECT. The therapy owls are the worst-injured owls. They'd be released less often no matter what, so the lower release rate doesn't show the therapy fails. The vets can be right that it improves each owl's chances.

questions.stimulus: Ferry operator: Our two routes across Mell Sound are the same length, and the boats on the eastern route are newer and faster than those on the western route. Nevertheless, over the past year, eastern-route crossings arrived behind schedule much more often than western-route crossings did.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why eastern-route crossings arrived behind schedule more often than western-route crossings did?
choices: The eastern route's timetable allows considerably less time for each crossing than the western route's timetable does.
Storms disrupted crossings on Mell Sound more often during the past year than in any previous year.
The eastern route carries far more passengers in the summer months than in the winter months.
The older boats on the western route were taken out of service for repairs more often than the eastern route’s boats were.
Passengers on the eastern route complained about late arrivals more often than did passengers on the western route.
questions.explanation: Core move: see that 'behind schedule' is measured against each route's own schedule, not against the clock. If the eastern timetable gives each crossing much less time (A), faster boats can still miss it more often. The most tempting trap is B: bad weather does cause late arrivals, but the storms hit the whole sound, so they don't explain why one route ran late more than the other. D makes the western route look worse, deepening the puzzle, and E merely restates that the eastern route was late more often.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The eastern route has newer, faster boats on an equally long crossing, but its crossings arrived behind schedule more often than the western route's.

breakdown.analysis: Faster boats, same distance, more often late. Late compared to what? Compared to the schedule. Being 'behind schedule' depends on the boat's speed AND on how much time the timetable allows. Watch that relative word. We need an answer that says the eastern schedule is tighter. It's like a fast runner who misses a 10-minute target more often than a slow runner misses a 20-minute target.

choices.note: CORRECT. The eastern timetable is tighter. Fast boats facing a much tighter schedule can run late more often than slow boats on a generous one. Both facts fit.

Tempting. Storms really do make ferries late, so this feels like an explanation. But the storms hit Mell Sound, which both routes cross. A cause that affects both routes can't explain a difference between them. In a comparison paradox, you need something that differs between the groups.
Wrong comparison. This compares the eastern route with itself across seasons. The puzzle is eastern versus western.
Opposite. If the western route's boats were out for repairs more often, the western route should have had more trouble, not less. This deepens the puzzle.
This restates the puzzle. More complaints about lateness is just another sign that the eastern route ran late more. It doesn't say why.

questions.stimulus: To reduce the time its attorneys spend on initial interviews, the Hartsfield legal aid clinic began requiring every applicant to complete a detailed online intake form before being given an appointment. Since then, the average length of an initial interview at the clinic has increased, yet the total amount of attorney time spent on initial interviews has decreased.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Attorneys now use the information on the intake form to ask applicants more detailed follow-up questions during initial interviews.
Since the requirement took effect, the number of people applying to the clinic for help has increased.
Many applicants find the online intake form difficult to complete and ask the clinic's nonattorney staff for help with it.
The form screens out, before any interview, applicants with problems the clinic does not handle; such interviews had usually been brief.
Before the requirement took effect, many interviews were lengthy discussions with applicants who turned out to have problems the clinic does not handle.
questions.explanation: Core move: separate an average from a total. If the form screens out applicants the clinic can't help, there are fewer interviews, so total time falls; and because those screened-out interviews had usually been brief (D), removing them raises the average length of the ones that remain. Most students pick (E) because it also involves ineligible applicants, but it says their interviews were lengthy; removing long interviews would lower the average, so (E) explains the falling total while making the rising average harder to explain. (A) accounts for the longer average only, and (B) makes the falling total harder to explain.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: After the intake form was required, the average initial interview got longer, but total attorney time on initial interviews went down.

breakdown.analysis: Average up, total down. How? Total = number of interviews × average length. If the average went up, the number of interviews must have dropped enough to more than make up for it. And for the average to rise, the interviews that disappeared should be the short ones. Prephrase: the form eliminates interviews, mostly short ones. It's like a class average rising after the lowest scorers drop the course. Most students pick (E) because it's about screening out the wrong applicants too; but it says those interviews were long, and removing long ones would pull the average down.

choices.note: Explains half. Detailed follow-up questions would make interviews longer, but nothing here reduces the number of interviews, so the total should rise.
Deepens the puzzle. More applicants means more interviews; with each one longer, total time should go up.
Irrelevant. Nonattorney staff time on the form doesn't affect attorney interview time.
CORRECT. Fewer interviews → lower total. The ones removed were short → the average of the remaining ones rises. Both facts explained.

Tempting, and the main trap. It also has the form weeding out the wrong applicants, which explains the lower total. But it says those interviews were lengthy. Remove long interviews and the average should fall, the opposite of what happened.

questions.stimulus: Kite maker: Kites made with our new lightweight fabric can stay aloft in lighter winds than can kites made with our older, heavier fabric. Yet at last month's Carrow Kite Festival, where winds were light all day, more of our older-fabric kites than our new-fabric kites stayed aloft for the full hour of the endurance competition.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: Far more older-fabric kites than new-fabric kites were entered in the festival's one-hour endurance competition.
In strong winds, kites made with the older fabric generally stay aloft longer than kites made with the new fabric do.
The new fabric frays where it rubs against a kite's frame, so new-fabric kites often tear during flights longer than half an hour.
Most of the new-fabric kites in the endurance competition were flown by people who had never before competed at a kite festival.
Most new-fabric kites at the festival were flown on the heavy lines made for older kites, which cancel the new fabric's light-wind advantage.
questions.explanation: Core move: in an EXCEPT question, confirm that four choices resolve the puzzle and find the one that only sounds as if it does. (B) is about strong winds, but the festival's winds were light all day, so the older fabric's strong-wind edge can't explain these results. Most students pick (A) as the EXCEPT because it says nothing about fabric; but the stimulus says 'more of' the older kites stayed up, an absolute count, and if far more older kites were entered, more of them could stay aloft even if a larger share of the new kites did. (C), (D), and (E) each give a reason the new-fabric kites failed at this festival despite their light-wind advantage.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: New-fabric kites stay up in lighter winds than older-fabric kites, but in a light-wind endurance contest, more older-fabric kites lasted the full hour.

breakdown.analysis: EXCEPT question: four answers resolve the puzzle, one doesn't. So first, what kinds of answers resolve it? 1. Something else hurt the new kites at this festival (fraying, inexperienced fliers, wrong lines). 2. The comparison is a count, not a rate: 'more of' the older kites stayed up. If far more older kites entered, more of them could finish even with a worse success rate. Watch the count trap: it looks irrelevant, so people pick it as the EXCEPT. Most students do exactly that with (A). Read 'more of' carefully; it's a number, not a percentage.

choices.note: Tempting to pick, and the main trap. It looks like it has nothing to do with fabric. But the stimulus compares counts ('more of'). If 50 older kites and 5 new kites entered, 10 older finishers beats 4 new ones even though the new kites did better as a share. That resolves it.

CORRECT. This is the one that doesn't help. The festival's winds were light all day. An advantage in strong winds is irrelevant to what happened there. It sounds like a fabric difference that matters, but it's the wrong conditions.
Helps. The contest lasts an hour; if new-fabric kites tend to tear after half an hour, they'd fail the endurance test despite flying well in light wind.
Helps. Inexperienced fliers are a reason the new-fabric kites came down that has nothing to do with the fabric's ability in light wind.
Helps. Heavy lines cancel the new fabric's advantage, so at this festival the new kites had no light-wind edge.

questions.stimulus: Two months ago, Orwin Dairy covered the concrete floor of the pen where its cows wait to be milked with soft rubber mats. Since then, the average time it takes to move the herd through the milking parlor has dropped by nearly a fifth. The farm manager concludes that the mats, by making the cows more comfortable while they wait, have made them move more willingly into the parlor.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the farm manager's argument?
choices: How much did the rubber mats cost to purchase and install, and how long are they expected to last?
Do the cows produce more milk now than they did before the rubber mats were installed?
Are rubber mats also used in the waiting pens of other dairy farms in the region?
Do the farm's workers who move the cows prefer standing on the mats to standing on bare concrete?
Did the dairy change anything else about its milking routine when the mats were installed?
questions.explanation: Core move: an evaluate question about a causal claim asks you to check for another cause. If the dairy also changed its milking routine (new staff, new schedule, new gates) when the mats went in, that change could explain the faster milking; if nothing else changed, the mats look more likely to be the cause, so (E) matters either way. The most tempting trap is (B): more milk sounds like a sign of comfortable cows, but the conclusion is about moving into the parlor, and either answer leaves that unaffected.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The mats made the cows more comfortable and so more willing to move into the parlor.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Mats went in two months ago; time to move the herd through the parlor dropped by nearly a fifth.

breakdown.analysis: Faster milking after the mats. Was it the mats? Maybe the dairy also hired a better hand, changed the schedule, or fixed a sticky gate. A good evaluate answer has two answers that push opposite ways: 'yes, other changes' weakens; 'no, nothing else changed' strengthens. It's like crediting new running shoes for a faster mile; you'd want to know if you also started training. Prephrase: did anything else change at the same time?

choices.note: Irrelevant. Cost and durability tell you whether the mats were worth buying, not whether they caused faster milking.
Tempting, because more milk seems like a sign of happier cows. But the conclusion is about moving into the parlor. Milk yield could go either way without telling us why the cows move faster.
So? What other dairies use doesn't tell us what caused the change at Orwin.
Wrong group. The argument is about the cows' comfort, not the workers'.
CORRECT. If something else changed at the same time, it could explain the faster milking. If nothing did, the mats become the likely cause. Either answer moves the argument.

questions.stimulus: Last year the Drummond Regional Weather Service stopped describing the chance of rain as a percentage and began using phrases such as 'rain likely' and 'a slight chance of showers.' Since then, the number of calls the service receives from people asking what its forecasts mean has fallen by 40 percent. The service's director concludes that the new phrasing is easier for the public to understand than percentages were.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the director's argument?
choices: whether the number of people consulting the service's forecasts has changed much since last year
whether the service's forecasts have been more accurate this year than they were last year
whether the service consulted members of the public about possible wordings before adopting the new phrasing
whether the service's forecasters find the new phrases easier to write than the old percentages
whether other regional weather services in the area still describe the chance of rain as a percentage
questions.explanation: Core move: a count can fall because the pool shrank, not because the rate changed. Fewer confused callers supports the director only if roughly as many people still use the forecasts; if far fewer people consult them now, fewer calls would follow regardless of the phrasing, so (A) is what we need to know. The most tempting trap is (B): accuracy is about forecasts and sounds important, but the conclusion is about how understandable the phrasing is, not whether the predictions come true.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new phrasing is easier for the public to understand than percentages were.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the switch to phrases, calls asking what forecasts mean fell 40 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Fewer confused calls. Does that mean less confusion? Only if the same number of people are reading the forecasts. If half the audience moved to a phone app, calls drop with no change in understanding. It's like a store saying its new signs are clearer because fewer customers asked for directions, during a month when foot traffic fell by half. Prephrase: did the number of forecast users change?

choices.note: CORRECT. If far fewer people use the forecasts now, fewer calls would follow regardless of the phrasing. If the audience is the same size, the drop in calls is better evidence of clearer wording.
Tempting, because accuracy sounds central to forecasting. But the LSAT is specific: the conclusion is about understanding the wording, not about whether the predictions are right.
So? Asking the public first doesn't tell us whether the phrasing actually turned out easier to understand.
Wrong group. The argument is about the public's understanding, not the forecasters' convenience.
Irrelevant. What other services do says nothing about whether Drummond's change helped its own public.

questions.stimulus: Six months ago, the Brisco warehouse began paying its pickers a bonus for every order they fill beyond a daily quota. Since then, the number of orders filled per picker-hour has risen by 12 percent. The warehouse manager concludes that the bonus has made the pickers more productive.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the manager's argument?
choices: Has the warehouse hired additional pickers since the bonus was introduced six months ago?
Do most of the pickers regard the bonus as a fair reward for their extra effort?
Is the bonus paid to the pickers in each weekly paycheck or as a separate monthly payment?
Has the average number of items per order changed since the bonus began?
Have the warehouse's total shipping costs risen or fallen over the past six months?
questions.explanation: Core move: test whether the measure really tracks the thing concluded. 'Orders per picker-hour' counts orders, but an order can be one item or thirty; if orders got smaller, pickers could fill more of them with no extra effort, so (D) bears directly on whether the 12 percent rise reflects productivity. The most tempting trap is (A): more pickers sounds like it could inflate output, but the measure is already per picker-hour, so staffing levels are built into it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bonus made the pickers more productive.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the bonus began, orders filled per picker-hour rose 12 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Orders per hour went up. Is an order a fixed amount of work? No. If customers are now ordering two items instead of five, a picker fills more orders per hour while doing the same work or less. It's like a cashier bragging about serving more customers per hour in a week when everyone bought a single coffee. Prephrase: did the size of a typical order change?

choices.note: Tempting, because more staff usually means more output. But the measure is per picker-hour, so it already adjusts for how many pickers there are. Hiring doesn't change the comparison.
So? Whether pickers think the bonus is fair doesn't show whether their output really rose.
Irrelevant. How often the bonus is paid doesn't tell us whether productivity actually increased.
CORRECT. If orders got smaller, the 12 percent rise could happen with no gain in productivity. If order size held steady, the rise reflects real extra work. Either answer matters.
Too far removed. Total shipping costs depend on many things, like fuel, carriers and volume, and say nothing clear about pickers' productivity.

questions.stimulus: Choir director: Since we moved the Vellmar Youth Choir's rehearsals from Saturday mornings to Thursday evenings last spring, membership has grown by a third. Some parents credit the new music program at Vellmar's middle school for the growth. But that program did not begin until this fall, months after our membership started to climb. So the growth must be due to the rehearsal change.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the choir director's argument?
choices: whether the choir's membership had already begun to grow before the middle school's music program started
what share of the choir's new members joined only after the middle school's music program had begun
whether the parents who credit the music program have children who are enrolled in it
whether other youth choirs in the region hold their rehearsals on weekday evenings or on weekends
whether the Saturday morning rehearsals lasted longer than the Thursday evening rehearsals now do
questions.explanation: Core move: spot what a timing rebuttal leaves out. The director shows the growth began before the school program, but concludes that the rehearsal change explains all of it; if most new members joined after the program began, the program could account for much of the growth, and if few did, the rebuttal holds, so (B) cuts both ways. Most students pick (A) because timing is the heart of the argument; but the director already tells us the growth started months before the program, so asking it again settles nothing. (C) asks about the parents' motives, which can't show what caused the growth.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The membership growth is due to moving rehearsals to Thursday evenings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Membership grew by a third after the move; parents credit the school's music program; reply: the program began this fall, months after growth started.

breakdown.analysis: The program started after the growth began. Fine. But did the growth stop there? If most of the new members walked in this fall, the program could be the bigger cause, and the director only showed it wasn't the first cause. Prephrase: 'how much of the growth came after the program began?' A yes/no or high/low answer swings the argument either way, which is what an evaluate answer needs. Most students pick (A) because timing is the crux. But the stimulus already answers (A); a question whose answer we know can't help us evaluate.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap: it's about timing, the crux of the argument. But the director already told us growth started months before the program began. Asking it again adds nothing.

CORRECT. If most new members joined after the program began, the program could explain much of the growth and the conclusion ('must be due to the rehearsal change') fails. If almost all joined before, the rebuttal holds. Two-sided, and it targets the gap.
Parents' motives for their view don't tell us what caused the growth. Biased people can be right.
Other choirs' schedules say nothing about what drove this choir's growth.
Rehearsal length might matter to families, but either answer leaves open whether the program or the move drove the growth.

questions.stimulus: City engineer: Two years ago we widened the Corran Street bridge, adding a separate cyclist lane. Since then, collisions between cyclists and pedestrians on that bridge have fallen by 30 percent, while on the nearby, unwidened Mill Street bridge they have risen by 10 percent. Critics note that new lighting went up on Corran Street at the same time. But Mill Street received identical lighting that same month. So the widening, not the lighting, reduced collisions on Corran Street.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the engineer's argument?
choices: Was the new lighting on the two bridges installed mainly to reduce collisions or mainly to deter crime?
Has the combined number of cyclists and pedestrians crossing the two bridges changed over the past two years?
Has the share of the bridges' foot and bicycle traffic that uses Corran Street changed since the widening?
Are collisions between cyclists and pedestrians more likely to cause serious injuries than other collisions on the bridges?
Did the critics who cited the new lighting publicly oppose the widening project before construction began?
questions.explanation: Core move: the figures are counts, so ask whether traffic moved between the bridges. If many people switched from Corran Street to Mill Street, Corran Street's collisions would fall and Mill Street's would rise even if the widening did nothing; if each bridge kept its share, the comparison stands, so (C) matters either way. Most students pick (B), which differs by one idea: a change in the bridges' combined traffic would push both bridges' counts the same way and can't explain why they moved in opposite directions. (A) tempts because the lighting was the critics' point, but the rebuttal depends on what lighting each bridge got, not why it was installed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The widening, not the lighting, reduced collisions on Corran Street.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Corran Street collisions fell 30% while Mill Street's rose 10%; critics cite new lighting on Corran Street; reply: Mill Street got identical lighting the same month.

breakdown.analysis: Collisions are counts, not rates. So what if people simply moved? Two bridges side by side: if cyclists and walkers shifted from Corran Street to Mill Street, Corran Street's collisions drop and Mill Street's rise, with no help from the widening. Prephrase: 'Did traffic shift between the bridges?' If it did, the engineer's comparison is contaminated; if not, it stands. Most students pick (B), which is about traffic too, but about the total. A change in total traffic moves both bridges the same way; it can't produce one up and one down.

choices.note: The engineer's reply depends on which bridges got the lighting, not on why it was installed. Either answer leaves the comparison as it was.

Tempting, and the main trap: it's about traffic volume, the right neighborhood. But a change in the combined total would push both bridges' collision counts the same way. It can't explain why one fell and the other rose.

CORRECT. If Corran Street's share of the traffic fell, fewer people on it means fewer collisions and more people on Mill Street means more, regardless of the widening. If the share held steady, the opposite movements point to the widening. Either answer matters.
Severity is a different measure. The argument is about how many cyclist-pedestrian collisions occurred.
The critics' past views don't affect whether the lighting explanation is right. This is about the source, not the reasoning.

questions.stimulus: Every project funded from Dunmore's capital budget this year has been reviewed by the city's planning commission. The commission never reviews a project unless a completed environmental assessment of that project has been submitted to it, however small the project may be. The proposed Ash Street footbridge is funded from this year's capital budget.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: The planning commission has approved the plans for the proposed Ash Street footbridge after reviewing them.
Every project whose completed environmental assessment has been submitted to the commission has been reviewed by it.
Any project that the planning commission reviews is funded from Dunmore's capital budget for this year.
The Ash Street footbridge is the only capital project with an environmental assessment submitted to the commission.
A completed environmental assessment of the Ash Street footbridge has been submitted to the commission.
questions.explanation: Core move: chain two necessary conditions forward. Capital funding this year means the project has been reviewed, and a review requires a submitted environmental assessment, so the footbridge's completed assessment must have been submitted, which is (E). The tempting trap is (A), which swaps 'reviewed' for 'approved'; a review can end in rejection. (B) and (C) each reverse one of the rules.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Capital budget this year → reviewed by the commission; 2. Reviewed → completed environmental assessment submitted; 3. The footbridge is funded from this year's capital budget.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: capital budget → reviewed → assessment submitted. 'Never reviews unless' sets up a requirement: reviewed → assessment submitted. The footbridge is in this year's capital budget, so it rides the chain all the way. Prephrase: the footbridge has been reviewed, and its completed assessment was submitted. Watch for word swaps: reviewed isn't approved.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'reviewed' feels like 'approved'. It isn't. The commission might review the footbridge and reject it. The LSAT is ultra specific about words.
Reverses rule 2. A submitted assessment is required for review, not a ticket to one.
Reverses rule 1. Capital projects get reviewed, but the commission might review other projects too.
We don't know this. Every capital project this year had to have an assessment submitted, and other projects may have submitted one too. 'Only' claims are rarely supported.
CORRECT. Capital budget → reviewed → completed assessment submitted. The footbridge had to have one submitted.

questions.stimulus: Kayak club secretary: Most members of the Fenmoor Kayak Club own a dry suit. Every member who owns a dry suit takes part in the club's winter estuary paddle, which runs over several weekends. The winter paddle is held only on days when high tide falls in the early morning and the forecast calls for light winds.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the secretary's statements?
choices: Every member of the club who takes part in the winter estuary paddle owns a dry suit.
Members of the club who do not own a dry suit do not take part in the winter estuary paddle.
Most members take part in an activity held only on days when high tide falls in the early morning.
The club schedules most of its activities for days when high tide falls in the early morning.
Dry suits are more useful on the winter estuary paddle than on any of the club's other outings.
questions.explanation: Core move: carry a 'most' through an 'every' rule. Most members own a dry suit, every dry-suit owner joins the winter paddle, and the paddle is held only on early-high-tide days, so most members take part in an activity held only on such days, which is (C). The tempting trap is (B), which negates the rule: owning a dry suit guarantees taking part, but members without one might join the paddle too. (D) stretches one activity into most of the club's activities.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Most members own a dry suit; 2. Dry suit → takes part in the winter paddle; 3. Winter paddle → held only on early-morning-high-tide, light-wind days.

breakdown.analysis: Follow the majority: most members → dry suit → winter paddle. So most members do the winter paddle. And the paddle happens only when high tide is early (and winds are light). So most members do something held only on early-high-tide days. Dropping the wind condition is fine: 'only when A and B' still means 'only when A'. That's a 'most' carried through 'every' rules, which always works. Watch for the trap that negates the rule: no dry suit doesn't mean no paddle.

choices.note: Reverses rule 2. Dry-suit owners all paddle, but paddlers might include people who borrow a suit or rent one.
Tempting. It feels like the flip side of rule 2. But it's a negation error: dry suit → paddle doesn't mean no dry suit → no paddle. Anyone can join the paddle.
CORRECT. Most members → dry suit → winter paddle, and the paddle is held only when high tide falls early. So most members take part in an early-high-tide activity.
We only know about one activity. 'Most of its activities' stretches a single event into a scheduling habit.
Unsupported comparison. The secretary never compares how useful dry suits are on different outings.

questions.stimulus: At Ambrey Print Works, each apprentice is assigned either to the press room or to the bindery, but never to both. Every apprentice assigned to the press room has completed the shop's solvent-safety course. No apprentice assigned to the bindery teaches the Saturday letterpress class that the shop offers to the public.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: One of the apprentices who teaches the shop's Saturday letterpress class has not completed the solvent-safety course.
Some apprentice who has completed the shop's solvent-safety course is assigned to the bindery.
None of the apprentices who are assigned to the press room teaches the shop's Saturday letterpress class.
Some apprentices who have not completed the solvent-safety course do not teach any class at the shop.
Every apprentice who has completed the solvent-safety course teaches the Saturday class offered to the public.
questions.explanation: Core move: use an either/or rule to turn 'not one' into 'the other', then chain. An apprentice who teaches the Saturday class can't be in the bindery, so must be in the press room, so must have completed the solvent-safety course; (A) contradicts that. The tempting trap is (C), which sounds like it breaks the rules, but nothing requires any press-room apprentice to teach; maybe no apprentice teaches the class at all. (E) feels too sweeping, but it's possible: the facts never stop a course graduate from teaching.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Each apprentice: press room OR bindery, not both; 2. Press room → completed solvent safety; 3. Bindery → doesn't teach the Saturday class.

breakdown.analysis: Find the chain. Contrapositive of 3: teaches Saturday → not bindery. Rule 1: not bindery → press room. Rule 2: press room → solvent safety. So: apprentice teaches Saturday → press room → solvent safety. An apprentice who teaches on Saturday without the course is impossible. Everything else is loose. For a CANNOT question, the four wrong answers are just things that could happen.
