choices.note: CORRECT. Saturday teacher → not bindery → press room → solvent safety. An apprentice teacher without the course breaks the chain.
Could be true. Press-room apprentices must have the course, but nothing stops a bindery apprentice from taking it too.
Tempting, because it feels like someone has to teach. But nothing says any apprentice teaches the Saturday class. A senior printer might teach it. This can be true.
Could be true. Bindery apprentices may lack the course, and they don't teach on Saturday. Easy to picture.

Sounds extreme, but it's allowed. Picture a shop where only the press-room apprentices have taken the course and all of them teach on Saturday. No rule is broken. (It would fail only if some bindery apprentice had the course, and nothing says one does.)

questions.stimulus: App developer: Users of our Stride fitness app who switched on its optional daily reminder logged workouts on twice as many days, on average, as users who did not. Yet when we randomly selected half of the app's users to receive the daily reminder automatically, those users logged workouts on no more days, on average, than the users who were not selected.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the developer's statements?
choices: The daily reminder does not increase the number of days on which any user of the Stride app logs a workout.
Users who choose to switch on the reminder differ in some way, besides receiving it, from users who do not.
Most users who switched on the daily reminder would have logged workouts on just as many days had they not done so.
Users who switch on the daily reminder exercise more often than users who do not switch it on.
Sending the daily reminder to users automatically is less effective than letting each user decide whether to receive it.
questions.explanation: Core move: when a self-selected comparison shows a big gap and a random assignment shows none, the self-selected groups must differ in something besides the treatment. Whether choosers were simply more motivated or the reminder works only for people who want it, choosers differ from non-choosers in some way other than receiving the reminder, so (B) is supported either way. Most students pick (C) because it is the natural conclusion if choosers are just more motivated; it fails because the facts also fit a reminder that helps only the users who chose it, in which case most choosers would log fewer days without it. (A) is too strong for the same reason, and (D) swaps logging workouts for actually exercising.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Users who switched the reminder on logged workouts on twice as many days as users who didn't; 2. Users randomly given the reminder logged no more days than users not given it.

breakdown.analysis: Two comparisons, two results. The chosen-reminder group crushes the others; the randomly-reminded group doesn't budge. So what's special about the choosers? Two stories fit: 1. choosers are just more motivated, and the reminder does nothing; 2. the reminder works, but only for people who want it. Under either story, choosers differ from non-choosers in something besides the reminder itself. Hard to prephrase more than that; watch for answers that pick one story as if it were proven. Most students pick (C) because story 1 is the one that jumps out; it fails because story 2 is still on the table.

choices.note: Too strong. The random trial shows no average gain, but 'any user' is absolute. Under story 2 the reminder helps the users who want it.

CORRECT. Both stories require it: either choosers were more motivated, or they're the kind of user the reminder works for. Either way, they differ from non-choosers in some way besides receiving the reminder. Hedged, abstract, and true in every scenario.

Tempting, and the main trap: it's the obvious conclusion if choosers were just more motivated. But if the reminder works only for people who want it, choosers would log fewer days without it. The facts don't decide between the stories.
Wrong measure. The data are about logging workouts in the app, not about how often anyone exercises. Someone could exercise and never log it.
Not supported. The chooser gap may be pure selection, so we can't credit 'letting users decide' with any effect at all.

questions.stimulus: Every resident physician at Calder General who rotated through the intensive care unit (ICU) this year also rotated through the emergency department (ED). Most of the residents who rotated through the ED this year were first-year residents. No first-year resident rotated through the ICU this year, since hospital policy reserves ICU rotations for residents in their second year or later.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Some of the residents who rotated through the ED this year were in their second year of residency or later.
Most of the first-year residents at Calder General rotated through the ED at some point during this past year.
At least one resident who rotated through the ICU this year was in the second year of residency or later.
More of the residents who rotated through the ED this year skipped the ICU than rotated through it.
Every resident who rotated through the ED this year but was not a first-year resident also rotated through the ICU.
questions.explanation: Core move: combine 'most' with an exclusion to bound a subgroup. Every ICU resident also rotated through the ED and none was a first-year, so the ICU group sits entirely inside the non-first-year part of the ED group, which is less than half of it; the ED residents who skipped the ICU therefore outnumber those who didn't, which is (D) in roundabout wording. Most students pick (A) because 'most were first-years' seems to promise that some weren't; but 'most' is compatible with 'all,' and if every ED resident was a first-year, no one rotated through the ICU and (A) is false. (C) fails the same way, and (B) reverses the direction of 'most.'

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. ICU → ED; 2. Most ED residents were first-years; 3. ICU → not a first-year.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, but there's a structure. ICU residents are a subgroup of the ED residents, and they all come from the non-first-year slice. That slice is less than half of the ED group, so the ICU group is less than half of it too. Picture 10 ED residents, 7 of them first-years: at most 3 can have done the ICU, so at least 7 didn't. Now watch for answers that assume someone exists. 'Most' can mean 'all,' and then the ICU group is empty. Most students pick (A) for exactly that reason: it feels like 'most' leaves a leftover. It doesn't have to.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. 'Most were first-years' feels like it implies 'some weren't.' But 'most' includes 'all.' If all 10 ED residents were first-years, nobody did the ICU and this is false.
Reversed. We know most ED residents were first-years, not that most first-years were in the ED. Maybe there are 100 first-years and only 7 did the ED.
Same existence trap. If no one rotated through the ICU at all (possible if every ED resident was a first-year), there's no such resident.

CORRECT. ED residents who skipped the ICU include every first-year in the ED, which is more than half; ICU residents come only from the rest, which is less than half. So the skippers outnumber the ICU group. Awkward wording, airtight logic.
Too strong. Rotating through the ED and being a non-first-year doesn't put anyone in the ICU. Rule 1 runs ICU → ED, not the other way.

questions.stimulus: Someone who finds an injured wild animal should take it to a licensed wildlife rehabilitation center rather than try to care for it at home, unless no such center can be reached within a day. Home care, however well meant, too often does an injured animal more harm than good.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Marta cared for an injured heron at home for a week; since the heron recovered fully, she acted properly.
Jun drove a fledgling sparrow to a licensed center four hours away; he should instead have cared for it at home, where it would have been less frightened.
Priya should have taken the injured fox she found to a licensed center, even though the nearest one was a two-day drive away.
Tomas should not have kept the injured owl he found at home, since a licensed rehabilitation center was only an hour’s drive away.
Lena, a licensed rehabilitator, should release the hawk she has been treating as soon as it is able to fly.
questions.explanation: Core move: match the facts to the principle's rule and its exception. The rule says take the animal to a licensed center unless none can be reached within a day; Tomas's center was an hour away, so the exception doesn't apply and keeping the owl at home was wrong (D). The most tempting trap is A, because the heron's recovery makes Marta's choice feel justified; but the principle doesn't care how things turn out, and nothing says she couldn't reach a center. C gets the exception backward, since a two-day drive is exactly when home care is allowed.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Find an injured wild animal → take it to a licensed center, not home care. Exception: no center can be reached within a day.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: The right judgment must involve a center reachable within a day and say the animal belongs at the center (or a center out of reach and allow home care).

breakdown.analysis: Two parts: the rule (go to a licensed center) and the exception (no center within a day). The right answer has to line up with both. So what if things worked out? The principle is about what you should do, not how lucky you got. Look for someone near a center who kept the animal at home anyway, and a judgment that says that was wrong.

choices.note: Tempting. The heron recovered, so it feels like Marta did fine. But the principle doesn't judge by results. And we aren't told she couldn't reach a center, so the exception isn't triggered. Under the principle, she should have taken the heron to a center.
Opposite. Jun did exactly what the principle says: a center four hours away is reachable within a day. Calling that a mistake contradicts the principle.
This reverses the exception. A two-day drive means no center can be reached within a day, which is exactly when home care is allowed. The principle doesn't require the trip here.
CORRECT. The center was an hour away, well within a day, so the exception doesn't apply. The principle says the owl belonged at the center, so keeping it at home was wrong.
Irrelevant. The principle is about what someone who finds an injured animal should do, not when a licensed rehabilitator should release one.

questions.stimulus: Chess club president: Our club should not move its weekly tournament from Tuesday evenings to Saturday mornings. Admittedly, a survey shows that most members would prefer Saturday. But nearly all of our junior players have school sports on Saturday mornings and could not attend, while the members who prefer Saturday are all able to play on Tuesday evenings.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the president's reasoning?
choices: A club should schedule its regular events at whatever time the majority of its members say they prefer.
A change that would exclude some members should not be made just to suit members who could attend either way.
Club officers are not bound by the results of a survey of the club's members when making scheduling decisions.
Members who cannot attend an event because of other commitments should not have a say in when that event is held.
A club should survey all of its members before making any change to the schedule of its regular events.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the principle that takes the argument's facts and delivers its conclusion. The president's facts are that the move would shut out the junior players while the Saturday fans can play either day; B says that a change excluding some members should not be made just to suit members who could attend either way. The most tempting trap is C, because it seems to let the president set aside the survey; but freeing the officers from the survey doesn't tell them to keep Tuesday, so it doesn't justify the conclusion. A supports the opposite conclusion, and D would silence the juniors.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The club should not move the tournament from Tuesday evening to Saturday morning.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most members prefer Saturday (conceded); nearly all junior players couldn't attend on Saturday; everyone who prefers Saturday can still play on Tuesday.

breakdown.analysis: So most people prefer Saturday. Why isn't that the end of it? Because the president weighs a preference against being shut out. Moving the tournament would exclude the juniors just so others get the time they like better. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. We need: don't make a change that excludes some people just to satisfy the preference of people who can come either way. It's like refusing to move the family dinner to a time Grandma can't make just because the cousins would slightly rather eat later.

choices.note: Opposite. The majority prefers Saturday, so this principle would justify moving the tournament, not keeping it.
CORRECT. Moving to Saturday would exclude the juniors, and the only gain is suiting members who can play on Tuesday anyway. This principle says don't make that change, which is the conclusion.

Tempting. It sounds like it lets the president ignore the survey. But being free to ignore a survey isn't a reason to keep Tuesday. It doesn't tell the club what to do, so it can't justify the conclusion.
Opposite. This would take away the juniors' say, since they're the ones who can't attend on Saturday. It works against the president's reasoning.
Irrelevant. The club already surveyed its members. A rule requiring a survey says nothing about whether to move the tournament.

questions.stimulus: The Varn Seed Bank adds a seed sample to its permanent collection if, and only if, the sample passes a germination test and either belongs to an endangered species or comes from a population not yet represented in the collection. All other samples are returned to their donors.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: The marsh orchid sample should be added to the permanent collection, since the marsh orchid is an endangered species.
The red clover sample passed its germination test, so it should be added to the seed bank's permanent collection.
The dune grass sample comes from a population that is already represented in the collection, so it should not be added.
The wild oat sample passed its germination test but should not be added, since wild oat is not an endangered species.
The endangered cliff fern's sample passed its germination test, so it should be added even though its population is already represented.
questions.explanation: Core move: an 'if and only if' rule with one required condition plus an either/or condition; the right judgment must establish both. E has the germination test passed and the endangered branch of the 'either/or' satisfied, so the sample must be added, and the already-represented population doesn't matter. The most tempting trap is A, which satisfies the either/or condition but says nothing about whether the orchid sample passed its germination test. C and D each rule out only one branch of the either/or, so the other branch could still qualify the sample.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Added ↔ (passes germination test) AND (endangered OR population not yet represented).

setup.label: Application
setup.text: To say 'add', the judgment must show the test was passed AND one branch of the 'or'. To say 'don't add', it must show the test failed OR both branches fail.

breakdown.analysis: Two requirements: the test, plus one of two qualifiers. Every trap gives you only part. For 'add,' check: 1. passed the test? 2. endangered or new population? For 'don't add,' you need a failed test, or BOTH qualifiers missing. Ruling out one branch of an 'or' proves nothing.

choices.note: Tempting. Endangered satisfies the 'or' part. But we don't know whether the orchid sample passed its germination test, and that's required. Half the rule isn't enough.
Missing the second requirement. Passing the test isn't enough; the sample also has to be endangered or from a new population. We're told neither.
Rules out only one branch. Dune grass might be endangered, in which case an already-represented population doesn't matter. We can't say 'don't add.'
Rules out only the other branch. Wild oat isn't endangered, but the sample might come from a population not yet represented. If so, it qualifies.
CORRECT. Passed the test: yes. Endangered: yes, which satisfies the 'or'. So the rule requires adding it, and 'already represented' doesn't matter once the endangered branch is met.

questions.stimulus: Transit official: The Ostrey Island ferry should not be replaced by the proposed bridge. Admittedly, the bridge would shorten the trip for nearly all travelers and would cost less to maintain than the ferry. But building it would require demolishing the island's only harbor wall, and the island's fishing fleet, which supports a third of the island's households, cannot operate without that wall.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the transit official's reasoning?
choices: Savings in travel time and upkeep cannot by themselves justify a public project that would cost many of a community's households their livelihood.
A transportation project that would benefit nearly all of a community's travelers should be carried out unless it would deprive some residents of their livelihood.
A transportation project should be carried out only if it would benefit nearly all of the people who would use it.
When a ferry is replaced by a bridge, the people who worked on the ferry should be compensated for the loss of their jobs.
Decisions about public works on an island should be made by the island's residents rather than by officials on the mainland.
questions.explanation: Core move: the justifying principle has to deliver the official's verdict, 'don't build,' and conditional principles that only permit or only require something won't. The bridge's advantages are time and upkeep savings, and it would cost a third of the island's households their livelihood; (A) says such savings can't by themselves justify that kind of project, so the bridge shouldn't replace the ferry. Most students pick (B) because it mentions lost livelihoods; but 'should be carried out unless X' only tells you what to do when X is absent, so when X is present it yields no verdict at all. (C) states a necessary condition the bridge seems to meet, so it can't yield 'don't build' either.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The ferry should not be replaced by the bridge.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Concession) the bridge would save travel time and maintenance costs; but it would destroy the harbor wall, without which the fishing fleet that supports a third of households can't operate.

breakdown.analysis: Benefits: time and upkeep. Cost: a third of households lose their livelihood. Conclusion: don't build. We need a principle whose trigger matches these facts and whose output is 'don't build' (or 'the savings aren't enough'). A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. Watch the conditional direction: 'do X unless Y' tells you to do X when Y is false; it's silent when Y is true. Most students pick (B) because 'deprive residents of their livelihood' is right there; it fails because it never says what to do when that happens.

choices.note: CORRECT. The only benefits are time and upkeep savings, and the project costs many households their livelihood. By this principle the savings can't justify it, which is the official's verdict.

Tempting, and the main trap. It names the livelihood problem. But 'should be carried out unless Y' means 'not Y → carry it out.' Here Y is true, so the principle says nothing at all. It never says 'don't build.'
A necessary condition for building. The bridge seems to meet it (it helps nearly all travelers), so this can't produce 'don't build.'
Wrong issue. It's about compensating ferry workers after a replacement, not about whether to replace.
About who decides, not what should be decided. The official's reasoning doesn't depend on who makes the call.

questions.stimulus: The Brask legal aid clinic has two rules. No one may advise a client at the clinic unless he or she is a licensed attorney. A licensed attorney may advise any client, except that an attorney who has not completed the clinic's tenant-law training may not advise a client in an eviction case unless a trained attorney reviews the advice before it is given.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principles stated above?
choices: Because Oduya is a licensed attorney, she was permitted to advise a client in an eviction case without having her advice reviewed.
Because Pell has completed the clinic's tenant-law training, he was permitted to advise a client in an eviction case.
Hanley gave unreviewed advice to a client in an eviction case without violating the rules, so Hanley must have completed tenant-law training.
Because a trained attorney reviewed Marsh's advice in an eviction case before it was given, Marsh was permitted to give that advice.
Because Ibsen has not completed the tenant-law training, she was not permitted to advise a client in a security-deposit dispute.
questions.explanation: Core move: run the rules backward. Anyone who gives advice without breaking a rule must be a licensed attorney (rule 1), and an untrained attorney may give eviction advice only after review (rule 2), so Hanley, who gave unreviewed eviction advice legitimately, must have completed the training, which is (C). Most students pick (D) because it satisfies the review exception exactly; but it forgets rule 1, since only licensed attorneys may advise anyone and we aren't told Marsh is one. (B) makes the same mistake from the other side, and (A) ignores that Oduya may be untrained.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: 1. Advise a client → licensed attorney. 2. Untrained attorney advising in an eviction case → advice reviewed first by a trained attorney. Contrapositive of 2: eviction advice given without review (and permitted) → the attorney is trained.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: A 'permitted' judgment must show: licensed AND (not eviction OR trained OR reviewed). A 'must have' judgment must follow from the rules plus the stated facts.

breakdown.analysis: Two gates. Gate 1: are you a licensed attorney? Without that, nothing else matters. Gate 2 applies only to eviction cases: if you're untrained, your advice needs a trained attorney's review. Every trap clears one gate and forgets the other. Now run it backward: if someone gave unreviewed eviction advice and broke no rule, they passed gate 1 (licensed), and since there was no review, they must be trained. That's a contrapositive, the kind of awkward answer hard questions hide behind. Most students pick (D), which clears gate 2 perfectly and never mentions gate 1.

choices.note: Licensed clears gate 1, but this is an eviction case with no review. That's allowed only if Oduya is trained, and we aren't told she is. 'Licensed' alone doesn't permit it.
Gate 2 is fine, since trained attorneys don't need review. But the rules never say training makes you a licensed attorney. If Pell isn't licensed, he can't advise anyone.

CORRECT. No violation means Hanley is a licensed attorney. Eviction case, no review: under rule 2 that's forbidden for an untrained attorney. So Hanley must be trained. This follows strictly from the rules.

Tempting, and the main trap. The review satisfies rule 2 for an untrained attorney. But rule 1 comes first: only licensed attorneys may advise anyone, and we don't know Marsh is licensed. Review doesn't make a nonattorney eligible.
Wrong scope. A security-deposit dispute isn't an eviction case, so the training rule doesn't apply. If Ibsen is licensed, she may give this advice.

questions.stimulus: Every kite sold at Fenner’s shop is made of ripstop nylon, and every ripstop nylon kite comes with a one-year guarantee against tearing. So the kite Alma bought at Fenner’s shop comes with a one-year guarantee against tearing.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every ferry on the Selby route stops at Penn Island, and some ferries that stop at Penn Island carry cars. So the ferry Juno took on the Selby route carried cars.
Every play staged by the Linden Players is performed in the old granary, and every performance in the old granary is unamplified. So the play Tess saw the Linden Players stage was unamplified.
Every seed sample in the Hollin vault has been dried, and every dried sample has been tested for disease. So any sample that has been tested for disease is in the Hollin vault.
Every loom at the Abner mill is inspected monthly, and every loom that is inspected monthly runs reliably. So the Abner mill will not need to buy new looms this year.
No member of the chess club who plays in the spring tournament may skip the opening meeting, and Ren is a member of the chess club. So Ren will attend the opening meeting.
questions.explanation: Core move: match a simple chain, all A are B, all B are C, this item is an A, so it is C. B has exactly that: Linden play → granary → unamplified, and Tess saw a Linden play. The most tempting trap is A, which looks almost identical, but its second premise says only 'some' ferries that stop at Penn Island carry cars, so the chain breaks. C reverses the chain, D concludes something the premises never mention, and E leaves out the needed fact that Ren plays in the tournament.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Alma's kite from Fenner's comes with a one-year tear guarantee.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every Fenner's kite is ripstop nylon; every ripstop nylon kite has the guarantee; Alma's kite is from Fenner's.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; all B are C; this x is an A; so x is C. (Valid.)

breakdown.analysis: A clean chain: Fenner's → ripstop → guarantee. Alma's kite is a Fenner's kite, so it gets the guarantee. Find another 'all, all, this one, so' chain that runs the same direction. Check quantifiers: one 'some' in the middle breaks the whole chain.

choices.note: Tempting. Same shape on the surface. But 'some ferries that stop at Penn Island carry cars' is not 'all.' Juno's ferry could be one that doesn't. The chain breaks at 'some.'
CORRECT. Linden play → granary → unamplified. Tess saw a Linden play, so it was unamplified. Same valid chain, same direction.
Reversed. The premises say vault → dried → tested. The conclusion runs tested → vault, which is backward. It also concludes about a whole group, not about one item.
New idea in the conclusion. The premises are about reliable looms; the conclusion jumps to buying new looms, which nothing connects.
Missing link. The rule applies to members who play in the spring tournament. We're only told Ren is a member, not that he's playing.

questions.stimulus: A ferry crossing can leave on time only if the loading crew arrives early. The loading crew arrived early this morning. So this morning’s crossing left on time.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: A play can open on schedule only if its set is finished. The set for the new play was not finished. So the new play did not open on schedule.
If an injured owl's wing has fully healed, the owl can be released into the wild. This owl's wing has not fully healed. So this owl cannot be released into the wild.
A seed sample is stored in the cold vault only if it has been dried. This sample is stored in the cold vault. So this sample has been dried.
A loom can run at full speed only if it has been oiled. The east-floor loom was oiled today. So the east-floor loom is running at full speed.
Whenever the chess club meets on a Friday, attendance at its meeting rises. The club will meet on a Friday next week. So attendance at next week's meeting will rise.
questions.explanation: Core move: diagnose the flaw, then find the same flaw. The argument treats a necessary condition (the crew arriving early) as if it were sufficient for leaving on time; D does the same with oiling and full speed. The most tempting trap is B, which is also a flawed conditional argument, but its error is different: it assumes that failing a sufficient condition (a healed wing) rules out the result. A, C, and E are valid arguments, so they can't match a flawed one.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: This morning's crossing left on time.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Leave on time → crew arrives early; the crew arrived early.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X only if Y; Y happened; so X. (Treats a necessary condition as sufficient.)

breakdown.analysis: 'Only if' marks a requirement. On time → crew early. The crew showing up early means the crossing COULD leave on time; it doesn't mean it did. It's like saying 'you can pass only if you study; you studied, so you passed.' This is the necessary-versus-sufficient flaw. It's a classic; know it. Find the answer that meets a requirement and declares the result.

choices.note: Valid, so it can't match. Open on schedule → set finished. Set not finished, so not on schedule. That's the contrapositive, done correctly.

Tempting, because it's also a broken conditional. But it's a different break. Healed → can be released. Not healed, so can't be released: that denies the sufficient condition. The stimulus affirms the necessary condition instead. Same family, different flaw.
Valid. Cold vault → dried. In the cold vault, so dried. The arrow runs the right way.
CORRECT. Full speed → oiled. It was oiled, so it's at full speed. Same error: a requirement is met and the result is assumed to follow.
Valid. Friday → attendance rises. Next week is a Friday meeting, so attendance rises. The sufficient condition is met, so the result does follow.

questions.stimulus: Seed bank director: We will extend our opening hours only if we receive a state grant, and we will receive a state grant only if we hire a second archivist. Since we have decided not to hire a second archivist, we will not extend our opening hours.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?
choices: The Elm Street Theater will add a Sunday matinee only if its lead actor agrees, and she will agree only if paid extra. The theater cannot pay her extra, so it will not add the matinee.
The Harlan ferry will add a late sailing only if demand rises, and demand will rise only if fares are cut. Since fares are being cut next month, the ferry will add a late sailing.

The chess club will move to a larger hall if its membership grows, and its membership will grow if it offers a course for beginners. Since the club is offering a beginners’ course, it will move to a larger hall.

Tolland Airport will expand its terminal only if passenger numbers grow and the county approves funding for the work. Since the county has now approved that funding, the airport will expand its terminal.
The Calder mill will reopen its dye house only if it wins a new contract from a clothing maker. Since the mill will not win any new contract this year, it will not hire any new workers.
questions.explanation: Core move: map the chain and the direction of inference. The stimulus links hours → grant → archivist and then denies the last link to deny the first; A does exactly that with matinee → actor agrees → extra pay. The strongest trap is C, which is also a valid chain, but it runs forward from a sufficient condition to its result rather than backward by denying a requirement, so its pattern differs. B and D affirm necessary conditions, which is invalid, and E's conclusion introduces hiring, which the premise never mentions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The seed bank will not extend its opening hours.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Extend hours → grant; grant → second archivist; no second archivist.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A only if B; B only if C; not C; so not A. (Valid: a chain run backward through the contrapositive.)

breakdown.analysis: Chain: hours → grant → archivist. No archivist, so no grant, so no extended hours. That's the contrapositive run all the way back. A valid argument needs a valid match, and the same direction matters: this one denies the last requirement to deny the first thing. It's like: 'You'll get the job only if you interview, and you'll interview only if you apply. You didn't apply, so no job.'

choices.note: CORRECT. Matinee → actor agrees → paid extra. Can't pay extra, so she won't agree, so no matinee. Same chain, same backward direction.

Invalid. Late sailing → demand → fare cut. Fares are being cut, which only meets a requirement. It concludes the sailing will be added, which affirms a necessary condition. The stimulus is valid; this isn't.

Tempting. It's a valid two-step chain, so it feels like a match. But it runs forward: course → growth → larger hall, and the course is happening. The stimulus runs backward, denying the final requirement. Valid isn't enough; the pattern must match.
Invalid, and the structure differs. One requirement has two parts (growth AND funding), and only one part is met. Meeting part of a necessary condition proves nothing.
The conclusion is about hiring workers, but the premise is only about reopening the dye house. The conclusion doesn't connect to the premise at all.

questions.stimulus: Club secretary: Most members of the Glenmore Chess Club play in the club's Thursday evening league, and most of the players in the Thursday league are under thirty years old. So it is clear that most members of the Glenmore Chess Club are under thirty years old.
questions.stem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most closely parallel to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?
choices: Most passengers on the Selby ferry buy return tickets, and most passengers on the Selby ferry are island residents. So some island residents who ride the Selby ferry buy return tickets.
Most of the Abner mill's weavers work the night shift, and most of the mill's night-shift workers are union members. So most of the mill's union members are weavers.
Most kites sold at Pell's shop are box kites, and all box kites sold at Pell's shop are handmade. So most kites sold at Pell's shop are handmade.
Most of the owls admitted to the Fenwick wildlife center have wing injuries. So most owls with wing injuries are admitted to the Fenwick wildlife center.
Most flights at Tolland Airport are operated by Skyline Air, and most Skyline Air flights at Tolland depart before noon. So most flights at Tolland Airport depart before noon.
questions.explanation: Core move: 'most A are B, and most B are C, so most A are C' is invalid, because the B's that are C need not be the A's that are B (the Thursday league could be mostly young nonmembers). (E) repeats that skeleton exactly with flights, Skyline flights, and morning departures. Most students pick (C) because it reads almost identically, but its second premise says 'all,' and 'most A are B, all B are C' validly yields 'most A are C'; a valid argument can't match a flawed one. (A) is also valid, since two 'most' statements about the same group guarantee overlap, and (B) and (D) are flawed in a different way, by reversing a relationship.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most Glenmore club members are under thirty.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most members play in the Thursday league; most Thursday league players are under thirty.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; most B are C; so most A are C. (Invalid: the B's that are C may not be the A's.)

breakdown.analysis: Most members play Thursdays, and most Thursday players are young. So most members are young? Not necessarily. The Thursday league might be packed with young nonmembers (guests, students) while the members in it are the older ones. Quick numbers: 10 members, 6 play Thursdays; the league has 30 players, 24 under thirty, all of them nonmembers. Most A are B, most B are C, and no A is C. Now find the same chain: two 'most' links in a row. Most students pick (C), which looks the same at a glance; check the quantifier in the second premise.

choices.note: Valid, so it can't match. Two 'most' statements about the same group (passengers) must overlap: more than half plus more than half is more than all. So some residents buy return tickets.
Flawed, but differently. It reverses the direction of the conclusion (most union members are weavers) rather than chaining two 'most' links forward to 'most A are C.'
Tempting, and the main trap. Same shape, one word different: 'all box kites are handmade.' Most A are B, all B are C → most A are C is valid. A valid argument can't parallel a flawed one.
Flawed, but a different flaw: a simple reversal of one 'most' statement. There's no chain of two premises.

CORRECT. Most flights (A) are Skyline flights (B); most Skyline flights (B) leave before noon (C); so most flights (A) leave before noon (C). Same two-step 'most' chain, same gap. Numbers: 10 flights, 6 Skyline, 4 of those in the morning, the 4 others all in the afternoon. Then only 4 of 10 leave before noon.

questions.stimulus: Wildlife center director: Only people who have completed our bird-handling course are permitted to volunteer at the center, and every one of our volunteers is skilled at calming injured birds. It follows that anyone who has completed our bird-handling course is skilled at calming injured birds.
questions.stem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Everyone who volunteers at the Elm Street Theater must first attend a safety briefing, and Halla has never attended a safety briefing there. It follows that Halla does not volunteer at the Elm Street Theater.

Only students who pass the qualifying exam may join the Holt chess team, and every student who passes the qualifying exam has a rating above 1500. It follows that every member of the Holt chess team has a rating above 1500.

Every member of the Pell Street kite club owns a handmade kite, and no one may join the club without attending a kite-making workshop. It follows that no one who has attended such a workshop lacks a handmade kite.
Every pilot based at Tolland Airport is certified for night flying, and Ines has recently been certified for night flying. It follows that Ines must be one of the pilots based at Tolland Airport.

All of the Abner mill's dyers wear respirators at work, and all of the mill's dyers have completed its safety course. It follows that some people who have completed the mill's safety course wear respirators at work.
questions.explanation: Core move: the director has two facts that are each necessary for volunteering (the course, and calming skill) and wrongly concludes that one guarantees the other: course → skilled. (C) has the same structure in disguise, with its premises in the opposite order and its conclusion stated as a double negative: member → handmade kite, member → workshop, so workshop → handmade kite. Most students pick (B) because it copies the stimulus's opening words ('Only students who pass … may join'), but its second premise attaches the trait to everyone who meets the requirement, so join → pass → rating is a valid chain. (D) commits a related but different error, inferring membership from a single necessary condition.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Anyone who completed the bird-handling course is skilled at calming injured birds.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Volunteer → completed course; volunteer → skilled at calming birds.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All M are A (A is required for M); all M are B; so all A are B. (Treats a requirement for membership as if it guaranteed what members have.)

breakdown.analysis: Volunteers took the course. Volunteers are skilled. So everyone who took the course is skilled? Plenty of people could take the course, never volunteer, and be hopeless with birds. The course is necessary for volunteering, not sufficient. It's like: 'Only licensed drivers may drive for us, and all our drivers are excellent, so everyone with a license is an excellent driver.' Now hunt for the same skeleton. It may be scrambled: premises swapped, conclusion phrased as 'no one … lacks.' Most students pick (B), which matches the wording, not the logic.

choices.note: Valid, so it can't match. Volunteer → briefing; Halla had no briefing; so she doesn't volunteer. A correct contrapositive.

Tempting, and the main trap. It even opens with 'Only students who pass … may join,' just like the stimulus. But the second premise is about everyone who PASSES, not about members: join → pass → rating above 1500. That chain is valid. Same words, different logic.

CORRECT. Translate: member → handmade kite; member → attended workshop. Conclusion: 'no one who attended … lacks a handmade kite' = workshop → handmade kite. Two necessary conditions for membership, and one is treated as guaranteeing the other. Same flaw, reordered and phrased negatively.

Flawed, but a different flaw. It infers that Ines is a member (a Tolland pilot) from one necessary condition. The stimulus never concludes that anyone is a member; it concludes that one requirement guarantees another trait.
Valid. If all dyers both wear respirators and took the course, those dyers are people who took the course and wear respirators. It concludes only 'some,' which follows.

questions.stimulus: Fernley should restore the evening run of its harbor ferry. When the run was cut two years ago, the savings to the ferry service turned out to be small, while shops near the harbor reported that their evening customers fell by nearly half. Restoring the run would cost the town little and would help those shops recover.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: Cutting the evening ferry run saved the ferry service only a small amount of money.
Shops near the harbor lost nearly half of their evening customers after the evening run was cut.
The ferry service should not have cut its evening run two years ago.
Restoring the evening ferry run would help the harbor shops recover.
Fernley ought to bring back the evening run of its harbor ferry.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the claim everything else supports. The small savings, the shops' losses, and the low cost of restoring the run are all reasons for the recommendation in the first sentence, so E is the conclusion. The most tempting trap is C, which sounds like the arguer's view, but the argument never says the original cut was a mistake; it argues about what to do now. A, B, and D are premises offered in support of E.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Fernley should restore the evening ferry run.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The cut saved little; harbor shops lost nearly half their evening customers; restoring the run would cost little and help the shops recover.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. Small savings, lost customers, cheap to restore: why tell us all that? To show that Fernley should bring the run back. Here the conclusion comes first, which is common. Don't assume it's the last sentence.

choices.note: Premise. This is one reason to restore the run, not the point being argued for.
Premise. The shops' losses support restoring the run. They aren't the conclusion.

Tempting. It sounds like something the arguer believes. But the argument never says the cut was a mistake back then. It argues about what to do now. A conclusion about the past isn't this argument's conclusion.
Premise. Helping the shops is a reason for restoring the run, given in the last sentence. It supports the recommendation; it isn't the recommendation.
CORRECT. Every other statement is a reason to do this. It's the recommendation the argument exists to support.

questions.stimulus: Some board members want the Riverside Community Theater to stage only well-known musicals, on the grounds that familiar titles sell more tickets. But last season the theater's two original plays sold nearly as many tickets as its musicals did, and the plays cost far less to produce. So the theater should keep staging original plays alongside its musicals.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that familiar titles sell more tickets?
choices: It is the conclusion that the argument as a whole is intended to support.
It is a premise offered in support of the argument’s main conclusion.
It is a consideration offered in support of a proposal that the argument opposes.
It is evidence that the argument uses to show that the board members’ proposal would be costly.
It is an intermediate conclusion drawn from the evidence about last season’s ticket sales.
questions.explanation: Core move: separate the author's own reasoning from the reasoning of the view the author rejects. The claim about familiar titles is the board members' reason for staging only musicals, a proposal the argument opposes, so C is right. The most tempting trap is B, because the claim appears among the argument's premises; but it supports the board members' position, not the conclusion that original plays should stay. E fails because the ticket evidence pushes against that claim rather than establishing it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The theater should keep staging original plays alongside musicals.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Opposing view: stage only well-known musicals, since familiar titles sell more tickets; but the original plays sold nearly as many tickets and cost far less to produce.

breakdown.analysis: Whose claim is this? Not the author's. It's the reason the board members give for their proposal. The argument then pushes back with ticket and cost numbers. So the claim supports a view the author rejects. Watch for 'on the grounds that': it tells you you're hearing the other side's reasoning.

choices.note: No. The conclusion is that the theater should keep staging original plays, the last sentence. This claim is a reason for the opposite proposal.
Tempting, because the claim really is a premise for some conclusion. But for which one? It supports the board members' 'only musicals' proposal, not the author's conclusion. Wrong side.
CORRECT. 'Familiar titles sell more tickets' is the board members' reason for staging only musicals, and the argument opposes that proposal.
No. The cost point is that original plays are cheaper. This claim is about ticket sales, and the argument doesn't use it to show anything about the board members' proposal.
No. The ticket evidence cuts against this claim. The author uses it to show original plays sell nearly as well. Nothing is concluded from that evidence that familiar titles sell more.

questions.stimulus: Some textile historians claim that the Callan mill closed in 1912 because cheap imported cloth had driven down demand for its products. But the mill’s ledgers show that it received more orders in its final year than in any earlier year. The ledgers also record that the mill’s waterwheel was destroyed by a flood that spring and was never rebuilt. So the closure was most likely caused by the loss of the mill’s power source.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by
choices: arguing that because one proposed cause of an event cannot be confirmed, the event probably had no single cause
citing evidence that conflicts with a proposed explanation and offering an alternative explanation that fits the evidence
showing that the evidence on which the historians’ explanation rests is unreliable
conceding that imported cloth hurt the mill’s business but denying that it was severe enough to cause the closure
drawing a general conclusion about textile mills from the history of a single mill
questions.explanation: Core move: describe the argument's moves abstractly. It cites a record level of orders, which conflicts with the falling-demand explanation, and then offers the destroyed waterwheel as a better explanation, so B is right. The most tempting trap is D, because the argument does deny that imports caused the closure; but it never concedes that imported cloth hurt the mill at all, and its evidence suggests demand was strong. C fails because the argument attacks the historians' conclusion with new evidence, not the reliability of their evidence.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Callan mill's closure was most likely caused by the loss of its waterwheel.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Historians say falling demand from cheap imports caused it; but orders were at a record high in the final year; and a flood destroyed the waterwheel that spring and it was never rebuilt.

breakdown.analysis: Two moves. 1. Knock down the historians' explanation: if demand had collapsed, why were orders at a record high? 2. Offer a better one: the mill lost its power. That's the classic 'evidence against their cause, plus my alternative cause.' It's like: 'You say the restaurant closed for lack of customers, but it had a waiting list every night. It closed because the kitchen burned down.' Find the answer that describes both moves.

choices.note: Wrong. The argument doesn't say the historians' cause just can't be confirmed, and it doesn't conclude there was no single cause. It names one cause.
choices.example: Example of method: No one can confirm that the storm caused the bridge to collapse, so the collapse probably resulted from many factors together.

choices.note: CORRECT. Record orders conflict with the falling-demand explanation; the destroyed waterwheel is an alternative explanation that fits the facts. Both moves described.

Tempting, since the argument does undercut the historians. But it never says their evidence is unreliable. We aren't even told what their evidence was. The argument brings in new evidence that conflicts with their conclusion.
choices.example: Example of method: The historians rely on a trade report that was later shown to contain invented figures, so their account can't be trusted.

choices.note: Tempting, because the argument does deny that imports caused the closure. But it never concedes imports hurt the mill. Record orders suggest business was strong. Don't read in a concession that isn't there.
choices.example: Example of method: Admittedly, cheap imports cut into the mill's sales, but the losses were too small to force it to close.

choices.note: Wrong. The argument is about one mill and draws a conclusion only about that mill.
choices.example: Example of method: The Callan mill closed after losing its waterwheel, so most textile mills of that era must have closed for lack of power.

questions.stimulus: Seed bank administrator: Critics call our plan to keep duplicate samples at a second site a waste of money, noting that our main vault has not lost a sample in sixty years. The plan is admittedly expensive, but the critics are mistaken. A clean record shows little about a vault's vulnerability if the vault has never faced the threat it is least able to withstand, and ours has never endured a prolonged power outage, the event most likely to destroy a collection at once.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: The main vault's sixty-year record without losing a sample provides little evidence about how vulnerable the vault is.
A prolonged power outage is the event most likely to destroy a seed bank's collection all at once.
The plan to keep duplicate samples at a second site is more expensive than the critics acknowledge.
Despite its expense, the plan to keep duplicate samples at a second site is not a waste of money.
The seed bank should stop relying on its main vault to protect any of the samples in its collection.
questions.explanation: Core move: find a conclusion that is stated only as 'the critics are mistaken,' then translate it. The critics call the duplicate-site plan a waste of money, so saying they are mistaken means the plan is not a waste, which is (D); the rest of the argument supports that. Most students pick (A) because it is the most conclusion-like idea in the final sentence; but the point about the clean record is the reason given for thinking the critics are wrong, so it is an intermediate step, not the overall conclusion. (C) distorts the concession, and (B) is a premise.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics are mistaken: the duplicate-site plan is not a waste of money.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A clean record shows little if the vault never faced its worst threat; the vault has never endured a prolonged power outage, its worst threat; so its sixty-year record shows little (intermediate step).

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. 'The critics are mistaken' is supported by the point about the clean record, and the clean-record point is supported by the power-outage facts. So the main conclusion is 'the critics are mistaken,' but you have to translate it: the critics said the plan is a waste of money, so the conclusion is that it isn't. The concession ('admittedly expensive') is just a concession. Most students pick (A), the intermediate conclusion, because it sits at the end and sounds like a verdict.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It's a real conclusion, but an intermediate one: it's the reason the critics are mistaken, which then supports the overall point that the plan isn't a waste.
A premise. It's used to show the clean record doesn't prove much.
Distorts the concession. The administrator admits the plan is expensive; nothing says the critics underestimate the cost.
CORRECT. 'The critics are mistaken' translated: the critics' claim was that the plan is a waste of money, so the conclusion is that it isn't, despite the expense the administrator concedes.
Way beyond the argument. The administrator wants a backup site, not to abandon the main vault.

questions.stimulus: Airport director: Some residents blame Harwick Regional Airport's new night-flight curfew for the drop in the town's hotel bookings, since bookings began falling the month the curfew took effect. But if that timing were enough, we would also have to blame the curfew for the closing of the town's only cinema that same month, and no one does. Moreover, bookings fell that month throughout the region, even in towns whose airports have no curfew. So the decline is better explained by a regional factor.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that we would also have to blame the curfew for the closing of the town's only cinema?
choices: It describes a consequence that the residents' reasoning would commit them to and that the director takes to be unacceptable.
It is offered as evidence that the decline in hotel bookings had a cause other than the curfew.
It is a claim that the director concedes is true but argues does not bear on the main conclusion.
It is an intermediate conclusion offered in support of the claim that the decline is better explained by a regional factor.
It is an example of an event that, like the drop in bookings, resulted from a factor affecting the whole region.
questions.explanation: Core move: recognize a claim the author does not believe. The director says that if timing alone proved causation, the curfew would also have to be blamed for the cinema closing, 'and no one does'; the claim is an absurd consequence used to show the residents' reasoning proves too much, which is (A). Most students pick (B) because the claim does help defeat the residents; but it attacks only their inference, while the evidence of a different cause is the region-wide decline, not the cinema. (D) fails because the director rejects the cinema claim rather than building on it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The decline in hotel bookings is better explained by a regional factor than by the curfew.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Residents: bookings fell the month the curfew began; director: by that logic the curfew also closed the cinema, which no one believes; bookings fell region-wide, even near airports with no curfew.

breakdown.analysis: Does the director think the curfew closed the cinema? No. That's the point: 'and no one does.' The claim is the absurd result of applying the residents' reasoning (timing = cause) to another case. The author doesn't believe this; it's the absurd result used to sink the rule. Two moves in the argument: 1. show the residents' inference proves too much (cinema); 2. give positive evidence for another cause (regional decline). Most students pick (B) because the cinema claim does hurt the residents. But it hurts their reasoning, not their conclusion; the positive evidence of another cause is move 2.

choices.note: CORRECT. If timing were enough, the residents would have to blame the curfew for the cinema too. The director treats that as plainly unacceptable ('no one does'), so the residents' reasoning must be faulty.

Tempting, and the main trap. The cinema claim does damage the residents, but only by showing their inference proves too much. It's not evidence of another cause; the region-wide decline does that job.
The director doesn't concede it's true. Blaming the curfew for the cinema is exactly what the director says no one does.
The director doesn't believe it, so it can't be an intermediate conclusion. It's a consequence the director rejects.
Nothing says the cinema closed because of a regional factor. The cinema is used only to show the residents' reasoning proves too much.

passages.title: Cooperative Grain Elevators on the Carlin Plains
passages.text:
Between 1900 and 1920, farmers in the Carlin Plains region built more than two hundred cooperative grain elevators: tall wooden storehouses beside the railroad tracks where grain was weighed, graded, and loaded onto freight cars. Before the cooperatives appeared, most elevators in the region were owned by a few 'line' companies, each operating dozens of elevators along a railroad. Farmers had long complained that these companies graded their grain unfairly low and paid less than it was worth, and historians have usually explained the spread of the cooperatives as the farmers' response to these grievances.

The historian Ada Reinholt has argued that this explanation is incomplete. Grievances against the line companies, she points out, were widespread long before 1900, and several cooperatives founded in the 1890s failed within a few years. What changed after 1900, in Reinholt's account, was not the farmers' anger but their means of acting on it. Two developments were crucial. First, a 1903 law required the railroads to provide track space to any elevator meeting basic standards, ending a practice in which railroads, at the line companies' urging, had refused sidings to cooperatives. Second, the founding of a regional cooperative sales agency in 1905 gave small local cooperatives access to buyers in distant markets, which they had been unable to reach on their own.

Reinholt supports her account with records of where and when cooperatives were founded. In the two years after the 1903 law, new cooperatives appeared at nearly four times the rate of the preceding decade, and they clustered in towns along the rail lines that had most often refused sidings in the past. Cooperatives in towns that joined the sales agency, moreover, were far more likely than others to remain in operation for a decade or more. The line companies' grading practices, by contrast, changed little over the same period.

Reinholt's emphasis on law and organization is a valuable corrective, and her evidence about timing is difficult to dispute. Yet in one respect her account may lean too far in the other direction. A track-space law and a sales agency made cooperatives possible; they did not make farmers willing to invest their scarce savings in them. Local newspapers from the period suggest that a cooperative was often founded soon after a particular grievance, such as a disputed grading or a sudden cut in prices, galvanized a community. In one town, a cooperative was organized within a month of a line company's refusal to regrade a single disputed carload of wheat. The grievances that Reinholt treats as a constant background may thus have supplied the occasion for founding a given cooperative, even if new laws and institutions explain why such efforts now succeeded where earlier ones had failed.

passages.title: The Reused Blocks of Teodora Halm
passages.text:
The woodcut prints of Teodora Halm, made in the 1920s and 1930s in the market town of Vesk, have long puzzled collectors. Many of them show faint, ghostly lines, such as a fragment of a roofline or the curve of a face, that bear no relation to the image in which they appear. Halm cut her images into blocks of pearwood, and it is now known that she reused the same blocks repeatedly, planing away an old image and cutting a new one into the fresh surface. (A woodcut prints from the raised surface that remains after the artist cuts away everything meant to stay blank.) Because the planing was often shallow, traces of the earlier image sometimes survived and printed along with the new one, faint but unmistakable to a trained eye.

For decades, critics regarded these traces as accidents of poverty. Halm, they noted, sold her prints cheaply at the Vesk market and could rarely afford new wood; the ghostly lines were thus flaws she tolerated rather than effects she sought. On this view, the most valuable impressions are the cleanest ones, and several museum catalogs have described prints with prominent traces as 'compromised.'

The art historian Jonas Remmet has recently argued that this judgment misreads Halm's practice. Remmet observes that Halm's account books, which survive for nearly every year of her career, show that she bought new pearwood at least twice a year, even in her leanest periods, yet she went on planing and recutting her oldest blocks. More tellingly, the traces are not randomly distributed. In a series of market scenes from 1931, the faint outline of the town's demolished grain hall appears behind the stalls in print after print, positioned with evident care, as though the vanished building still stood behind the market. Remmet concludes that Halm came to use the traces deliberately, as a way of letting the town's past show through its present.

Remmet's argument is strongest where it rests on the 1931 series, in which the placement of the traces is difficult to explain as accident. It is weaker as an account of Halm's work as a whole. Many earlier prints carry traces that seem to have no connection to the subjects of their images, some of them cutting awkwardly across a figure's face, and Halm's letters, which discuss her methods at length, never mention the traces at all. The likeliest story is that a technical necessity gradually became an artistic resource: Halm began by tolerating the traces and ended by composing with them. If so, the catalogers' habit of ranking impressions by their cleanness is mistaken, not because every trace is intentional, but because some are, and no single standard of value can be applied across her entire career.

passages.title: Handwriting Experts in the Courts of Tarland
passages.text:
In the province of Tarland, a witness may give expert testimony comparing a disputed document with samples of a person's known handwriting if the court finds the witness qualified 'by knowledge, skill, training, or experience.' Tarland's courts have interpreted this standard generously. A witness who has worked for some years as a document examiner, and who can describe the features examiners compare, such as letter proportions, the slant and pressure of strokes, and the ways letters are joined, is ordinarily permitted to testify and to tell the jury whether, in the witness's opinion, the defendant wrote the document in question. Opposing counsel may cross-examine such a witness, but challenges to the admissibility of the testimony itself rarely succeed; questions about its weight are left to the jury.

The legal scholar Mirela Vasko argues that this standard asks the wrong question. Whether a witness is experienced, she observes, says nothing about whether the comparisons the witness performs actually distinguish one writer from another. An experienced practitioner of an unreliable technique is not thereby made reliable; experience may simply make the practitioner more confident. Vasko proposes that Tarland's courts admit handwriting testimony only from examiners who have passed blind proficiency tests, in which examiners compare samples whose true authorship is known to the test's designers but not to the examiners, and that each examiner's error rate on those tests be disclosed to the jury.

Vasko's critique is well founded, and her proposal would be a considerable improvement on current practice. A 2011 study commissioned by Tarland's bar association found that examiners who had testified in Tarland's courts reached conflicting conclusions in nearly a fifth of the test comparisons they were given, yet each of them had been admitted on the strength of experience alone. A standard that cannot screen out disagreement on that scale is not doing the work an admissibility standard exists to do.

Still, proficiency testing addresses only part of the difficulty. An error rate measured on test samples describes how an examiner performs on the kinds of comparisons the test contains. Disputed documents in actual cases, however, often involve brief signatures, deliberately disguised writing, or writers whose hand has changed with age, conditions under which an examiner who performs well on ordinary samples may perform far worse. A low error rate disclosed to a jury could thus lend an examiner's opinion in a difficult case more weight than it deserves. Vasko's proposal would be strengthened by requiring that proficiency tests include comparisons resembling the one at issue in the case or, where no such tests exist, that the examiner be limited to describing the similarities and differences between the samples without offering an opinion on who wrote the document.

passages.title: Kin Recognition in the Roots of Carrowa
passages.text:
When two plants of the coastal annual Carrowa littoralis share a pot, each typically invests more of its biomass in roots than a plant grown alone, a response ecologists interpret as competition for soil nutrients, since a plant with more roots captures a larger share of a limited supply. In 2009 the botanist Ines Valdt reported a twist: the increase was much smaller when the two plants grew from seeds of the same mother plant than when they grew from seeds of different mothers. Valdt proposed that Carrowa recognizes kin through chemical cues released by roots and restrains its competitive investment when its neighbor is a relative, a restraint that would benefit the plant's genes, many of which its siblings share.

The proposal met immediate resistance. Critics noted that siblings resemble one another not only in their genes but also in their size and rate of growth, since they develop from seeds provisioned by the same parent plant under the same conditions. Two plants of similar size, the critics argued, may simply compete on more equal terms, so that neither is pushed into the steep root investment that a smaller plant makes when it finds itself beside a larger one. On this account, the pattern Valdt observed would arise from size matching, with no recognition involved. Valdt's original pairs, they pointed out, had not been matched for size.

Valdt responded with experiments designed to separate the two explanations. First she paired siblings and nonsiblings that had been matched for seed weight and early growth, and found that the difference in root allocation persisted. She then grew plants singly in soil that had previously held either a sibling or a stranger for several weeks, with the earlier plant's roots removed but any compounds they had secreted left in place. Plants in stranger-conditioned soil produced more roots than those in sibling-conditioned soil, though the difference was only about half as large as in the paired trials.

These results make size matching an unlikely explanation for the effect, but they leave the recognition hypothesis less complete than Valdt sometimes suggests. That conditioned soil reproduced only part of the response implies that root secretions, though they evidently carry some information about a neighbor's identity, are not the whole mechanism; contact between living roots, or cues that degrade soon after a plant is removed, may account for the remainder. Nor do the experiments show that restraint toward siblings actually benefits a plant's genes. A plant that grows fewer roots beside a sibling might leave nutrients for the sibling to capture, but it might equally leave them unused, and only a comparison of the combined seed production of sibling and nonsibling pairs could tell which.
passages.subject: natural-science

passages.title: Filling Losses in Medieval Wall Paintings
passages.text:
When a medieval wall painting has lost patches of its paint layer, through damp, flaking, or the careless removal of later plaster, a conservator must decide what, if anything, to put in the gaps. Few conservators today would repaint the missing areas in imitation of the original, a once-common practice now generally rejected because it passes off a modern conjecture as medieval work. The live dispute concerns the gentler alternatives. Some conservators favor fills that reconstruct the missing image in a technique detectable on close inspection, such as tratteggio, in which the fill is built up from fine parallel strokes that merge with the surrounding image at a distance but reveal themselves up close. Others hold that losses should be left as bare plaster or toned in a single neutral color, so that nothing is added that the painter did not put there.

The conservator Ilse Brandvold, defending the second position in her treatment of the chapel at Sankt Orm, has argued that distinguishability is a weaker safeguard than its advocates suppose. A fill that can be told from the original only by a viewer who stands close and looks for it is, for the great majority of visitors, who see the walls from several meters away, simply part of the picture. What such fills protect, she contends, is the conservator's honesty, not the viewer's understanding. Her opponents reply that bare losses do damage of their own. A large gap near the center of a composition does not present itself to the eye as an absence; it reads as a shape, often the most prominent shape on the wall, so that the viewer's attention is drawn to precisely the part of the painting that no longer exists. Leaving a loss bare, on this view, is not abstaining from interpretation but substituting one distortion for another.

Each side is right about the other and wrong about itself. Brandvold's objection to tratteggio holds wherever a fill must supply something the surviving fragments do not determine, such as a face whose features are wholly lost, because there even a distinguishable fill presents the conservator's invention with the authority of the image around it. But where a loss interrupts a pattern or a fold whose course is fixed by what survives on either side, a fill adds nothing that the painting itself does not already state, and Brandvold's worry lapses. Her opponents' point about bare losses, conversely, is strongest for exactly these small, determinate gaps, and weakest for the large ones, where any fill would have to invent. The question, then, is not which treatment is more honest in general but whether a given loss is one that the surviving painting can itself fill.
